articles.title: Dems admit uncomfortable election sweep truth as party descends on Denver to shape 2028 without a frontrunner
articles.summary: Pete Buttigieg, Josh Shapiro and other 2028 presidential hopefuls gather in Denver to debate the Democratic Party's direction after midterm wins.
articles.body: DENVER — Fresh off sweeping midterm victories, Democratic leaders, strategists and potential 2028 presidential contenders are heading to Colorado to debate what comes next for their party. The three-day "What’s Next" conference in Denver, organized by the independent group Majority Democrats, will bring together a broad slate of leaders from within the party as an advisor for the group admitting to Fox News Digital that the election results do not prove "validation of our party," but is more a "repudiation of Donald Trump." The conference organizers hope to bring together Democrats to see "where our party goes from here." The lineup includes former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran in the Democratic presidential primary in 2020; Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro; Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas; New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill; Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger; Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.; and former Obama advisor David Axelrod. KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY Democrats, as they prepare to take control of Congress in January, are seeking to capitalize on their electoral gains and strategize on how to make good on the campaign promises that won them control of both chambers of Congress and many usually red state Houses — like affordability and healthcare. Organizers describe the gathering as a chance to assess the 2026 results and discuss the leaders, ideas and debates that could shape the party through 2028 and beyond. The conference was scheduled even before Democrats' sweeping midterm victories earlier this month, when they saw historic seat flips not just in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. Democrats must now turn those midterm gains into a governing agenda that reaches beyond their energized base. Party leaders have pledged to lower costs, improve government services and investigate the Trump administration, but the party still faces questions about how to unite its progressive and moderate wings. VOTERS PUNISHED THE GOP OVER COSTS; NOW, DEMOCRATS FACE THE AFFORDABILITY TEST The conference is not an official Democratic Party event. Hosted by Majority Democrats, a group led by Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass., it is billed as an "independent, outsider conversation" about the party’s future. Lis Smith, a longtime Democratic strategist and veteran of several presidential campaigns, serves as a senior adviser to the group and said the post-midterm election event would take an honest look at the party’s recent victories and what comes next now that they will control the House and the Senate. "Democrats won big last week, but let’s be honest: the election was more a repudiation of Donald Trump than a validation of our party," Smith told Fox News Digital. "That’s why Majority Democrats is bringing together some of the biggest names and brightest new voices in Democratic politics at ‘What’s Next’ to have honest conversations about what worked, what didn’t and where our party goes from here." "This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to redefine what it means to be a Democrat, and our party can’t afford to squander it," she added. The conference’s high-profile guest list could also offer an early glimpse of the party’s 2028 presidential field, fueling speculation about who may seek the nomination. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With no clear frontrunner, the gathering gives potential contenders a chance to share their views as Democrats consider who might lead the party’s next campaign. For now, their more immediate test will be delivering on the promises that helped them win the midterm elections.

articles.title: Who is Scott Colom, Mississippi’s first Black senator in 150 years?
articles.summary: Mississippi is home to a large Black American population but no Black person has held a Senate seat since the 1800s.
articles.body:
United States prosecutor and Democrat Scott Colom has made history in Mississippi by becoming the deeply conservative state’s first Black senator in more than 150 years and ushering in the first Democratic victory there in more than four decades.

Senator-elect Colom’s narrow victory against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith was declared late on Wednesday, more than a week after the US midterms, which many have called a “blue tsunami” as Democrats firmly seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives.

It has been 43 years since Democrats last won a Senate seat in the state, in 1982.

But Colom’s win is significant beyond party politics and marks a turning point for Mississippi’s African American community too: he’ll be the first Black American senator since 1874.

It was a narrow victory. Colom beat Hyde-Smith, the incumbent and an ally of President Donald Trump, by fewer than 5,000 votes after 99 percent of ballots had been counted late on Wednesday.

Hyde-Smith had been ahead in polling for Mississippi, where Trump won by 23 points in 2024.

Colom’s win puts Democratic Senate control at 55-44. Another tight race in Alaska is still being counted, although Democrat Mary Peltola is also leading there by a slim margin.

Only 14 Black senators have ever been elected or appointed in the US. Colom will be one of seven new Black senators.

On Wednesday, after the results were called, Colom told supporters at his victory party in Jackson that he had come close to giving up.

“There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” the politician said, speaking at the historically Black Tougaloo College.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

Colom continued to thank his supporters in a series of messages on X on Thursday. “This victory belongs to all of us, and I am honored to be your new senator-elect,” he posted.

Colom, 43, is a lawyer who has served as a Mississippi prosecutor since 2016 until this year. He is married to Nadia Colom and has two children. His identical twin brother, Andrew, played a major role in his campaign.

The politician was born in Columbus and comes from a family of lawyers. Despite having one of the largest populations of Black Americans in the country, there has not been a statewide elected Black official in more than 140 years in Mississippi.

In interviews, Colom has said he decided to run to “look out for the people”, especially on the issue of affordability. He accused incumbent Hyde-Smith of neglecting the state and “selling out” Mississippians.

In 2015, Colom became the first Black American to be elected as district attorney for the 16th Judicial District, which includes the white-majority counties of Clay, Lowndes, Noxubee and Oktibbeha.

One of his most notable cases was Eddie Lee Howard, a Black American man who had spent 26 years on death row for murder but was released in 2021 as a result of a lack of evidence. After a judge dismissed the murder charge against him, Colom confirmed that prosecutors were dropping it.

In 2022, Colom was nominated as a US district judge by ex-President Joe Biden, but his nomination was blocked by Hyde-Smith, who claimed he was supporting transgender athletes and that he received funding from left-wing billionaire George Soros.

How did Colom win over Republican voters?

Many have credited Colom’s endearing personality, his respectful rhetoric, and especially his simple but effective campaign advertisements that supporters say are both funny and thought-provoking. He naturally appealed to Black voters, but also managed to reach the white majority.

In one advertisement, Colom played on his opponent’s weaknesses. In February, a TV reporter had asked Hyde-Smith, a rancher, how Republicans were attempting to address rising beef prices amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Hyde-Smith suggested that Mississippians find alternatives. “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she said.

The response drew outrage. Colom’s advertisement called on people not to pick another protein, but to “pick another senator instead”.

Colom’s wife, Nadia, featured prominently in the campaign. In one advertisement, just as Colom tells a reporter he does not have a nickname, Nadia appears and calls him “Sweet Thang”.

Colom’s final campaign video struck a more melancholy tone.

He invoked the memory of Medgar Evers, a US Army veteran and civil rights advocate who fought for the US in Normandy during World War II and returned home to fight racism during the Civil Rights Movement when Black people were pushing for the right to vote and to use restaurants or public restrooms. Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.

Across social media channels, many Mississippians who claimed they or their families usually voted for Republicans said they had gone out to vote for Colom in the midterms.

What are Colom’s positions on major issues in the US?

Affordability and better wages: Colom condemned the deeply unpopular Iran war, which has driven up grocery and gas prices. He has promised to push for more Congress involvement in future wars, fight for the Senate’s control over tariffs, and advocate for a rise in the minimum wage. He also promised to cut federal taxes for Mississippians earning less than $75,000.

Healthcare and safety: Colom promised to push back on the Trump administration’s efforts to cut Medicaid, back better pay for law enforcement officials, and push for secure borders while respecting the law.

Big Tech: Mississippians will decide on whether data centres can be constructed in their communities, while tech companies must pay for their own power and water for such facilities, Colom has said. He has also promised to push for better accountability for artificial intelligence.

Are there whispers of a Colom presidency?

Yes. Some of Colom’s supporters are already envisioning him in the White House in 2028, as Democrats jostle to field a viable candidate.

Some conservatives have called Colom a “bigger threat” than Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is also being named as a potential candidate.

But Colom has dismissed the conversation, saying his focus is on Mississippi.

“I am not trying to be a threat to anybody,” Colom told CNN.

“I’m trying to focus on delivering for Mississippi … We’ve got to get back to leadership that’s rooted in serving people, listening to them, learning their concerns, and delivering for them.”

articles.title: Trump’s Yalta: Witkoff and Kushner get played yet again in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: Witkoff and Kushner have no business leading these talks.
articles.body:
Wittingly or not, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were outplayed by Team Russia during the trilateral peace talks just held in Abu Dhabi between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia.

Moscow didn’t attend to negotiate peace in Ukraine. Rather, Russian President Vladimir Putin saw an opening — gullibly handed to him by Witkoff and Kushner — to undermine European unity and to attempt to lay the groundwork to reshape NATO.

Putin has long falsely argued that NATO’s expansion eastward was the root cause of his invasion of Ukraine. In 2021, he penned a lengthy essay titled, “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians,” accusing the West of intentionally turning Ukraine into an “anti-Russia” cause.

“Step by step, Ukraine was dragged into a dangerous geopolitical game aimed at turning Ukraine into a barrier between Europe and Russia,” he wrote. Putin also argued that Ukraine was being prepared as a NATO “springboard against Russia.”

Of course, it was entirely nonsense. Much of the essay, whose main points Putin regurgitated during his interview with the naive Tucker Carlson at the Kremlin, focused on overemphasizing Russia’s connection to Kyivan Rus — a Ninth century medieval Slavic state centered in Kyiv.

Putin’s need to co-opt Kyiv’s history as Russia’s own was necessary to argue that Ukraine is Russia. That said, it is important to understand that Putin’s contrived Russian history lessons are simply a smokescreen.

Putin’s war against Ukraine is in reality a war against the West and against NATO in particular. NATO, as currently constituted, is the biggest obstacle preventing Putin from reconstituting the Warsaw Pact.

Under the guise of peace talks, Abu Dhabi gave Putin an opening to attack NATO and the 32 member states that comprise the defensive pact that has kept the peace in Western Europe since the end of World War II.

Foolishly, Witkoff and Kushner fell into Putin’s trap when they strong-armed European NATO allies into agreeing to discuss Europe’s security architecture after the end of the war in Ukraine. That is, of course, code for NATO. In other words, Witkoff and Kushner put NATO’s future on the negotiating table — in effect agreeing to give Russia a say in what it looks like.

All 32 nations of NATO will get a vote on the outcome, and their approval isn’t likely. But this offer still plays into Putin’s false narrative that NATO caused Russia’s aggression in Eastern Europe. Equally bad, President Trump’s special peace envoys agreed to relegate European allies to the sidelines in Abu Dhabi. They were there, they just could not be in the negotiating room as Witkoff and Kushner acceded to the Kremlin’s refusal to include them.

In shades of the disastrous Yalta Conference in 1945 that led to the Iron Curtain and the Cold War, Team Trump negotiated with Russia over the fate of Europe and by extension the fate of NATO.

Vladimir Medinsky, Russia’s chief negotiator in Abu Dhabi, could not suppress his glee at dividing Ukraine and the U.S. from their European allies. He belittled the European contingent , which included Geoffrey Van Leeuwen , chief of staff to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and suggested that they act like tourists and meet at a bar.

Russia has made clear that Moscow is gunning for Europe. Earlier this week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated during televised remarks, that it was perfectly “reasonable” for Moscow to discuss Europe’s post-war security infrastructure. He sees it as a means to weaken it.

Moscow acts as though it is negotiating from a position of strength. But in reality, its army is getting wiped out in Ukraine — 1.6 million casualties so far and 2,580 in a single day this week .

There is nothing reasonable about Russia having a say-so, let alone a veto, over NATO’s future. Putin’s power play was more than obvious. We called it out several days before the Abu Dhabi talks began. Why couldn’t Witkoff and Kushner see what we did?

Europe as a whole certainly sees it. Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s High Representative, saw through Putin’s gamesmanship.

“So far, they have just been pretending that they negotiate,” she said. “We already have a European security architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their respective roles.” She then one-upped Putin by adding, “We must also make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture.”

Fortunately, on the U.S. side, there was one man at the peace talks who saw it as well: NATO Supreme Allied Commander Gen. Alexus Grynekewich, who also serves as commander of the U.S. European Command.

During his Senate confirmation hearings, Grynekewich said of the conflict, “I think Ukraine can win.” He also stated on TVP World this week that Ukraine is “essential to Euro-Atlantic security.”

Grynkewich should be leading these talks, not Witkoff or Kushner. His job is to defend NATO and not to sell it out to Putin.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Peltola campaign loses in court on rejected absentee ballots as she maintains narrow lead
articles.summary: Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola lost her court bid for ballot records and saw her narrow Alaska lead over Dan Sullivan shrink Wednesday.
articles.body: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola lost in her legal effort to get access to records identifying rejected absentee ballots during the ongoing count, and then lost some of her narrow lead in the latest ballot drop Wednesday night. An Alaska judge on Wednesday ruled against the Peltola campaign’s request for the records in the midterm's final uncalled Senate race, ruling the demand was "simply not reasonable" while election officials continue counting votes. Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews sided with the Alaska Division of Elections, finding the agency is "currently busy processing ballots from the 2026 general election" and "simply lacks the capacity to generate the report" from the voter registration database. "Even if the request were otherwise considered reasonable outside the peak election time of year, it is simply not reasonable nor required right now," Matthews wrote, adding that "the timing of the Campaign’s request could simply not be worse." MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT Peltola’s campaign had sued last week seeking information about which absentee ballots were flagged for rejection and why. Campaign attorney Abha Kelly told the court the process was "going incredibly smoothly" and that the campaign was not seeking confidential data or trying to disrupt the count. She argued the request would simply centralize transparency that observers already have in a decentralized way. DUNLEAVY CALLS ALASKA VOTING SYSTEM ‘VERY CONFUSING’ AS RAZOR-THIN SENATE RACE FROZEN IN TIME State attorneys countered that the records are not public, citing voter privacy interests. "Voters have a privacy interest in that because people who want to vote absentee presumably don’t want to mess it up and don’t want to be publicly exposed as having messed that up," Assistant Attorney General Margaret Paton-Walsh said. PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING' The state also said producing a customized report would impose a significant burden during peak election work. Matthews added at the Tuesday hearing that the case was "not about who won or lost the election" but about access to public records under the Public Records Act. The Sullivan campaign was allowed to intervene. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With roughly 86% of the expected vote counted and more than 248,000 ballots tallied, Peltola held 121,487 first-choice votes (48.9%) to incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's 117,512 (47.3%), a lead of 3,975 votes. Neither candidate is above 50%, so the race remains on track for ranked-choice tabulation after absentee counting concludes around Nov. 18, with certification expected Nov. 25. The race could still come down to the other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who has 4,100 votes, while Gerald Heikes has 5,426. Those third- and fourth-place totals exceed the current margin between the top two candidates and could prove decisive when lower finishers are eliminated and second-choice preferences are redistributed under Alaska’s ranked-choice system. The vote to repeal that voting system is failing at 52.5% to 47.5%, which is also still too close to call over a week after Election Day. Fox News' Melissa Chrise, Matt Finn, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump’s labor panel can free workers trapped in unions they oppose
articles.summary: Workers seeking to vote out a union they no longer want should not have to fight the government’s own rulebook to do it. Yet outdated agency-created barriers and union privileges still make such decertification elections harder to hold than they need to be — and harder than federal labor law says they should be. My…
articles.body:
Workers seeking to vote out a union they no longer want should not have to fight the government’s own rulebook to do it. Yet outdated agency-created barriers and union privileges still make such decertification elections harder to hold than they need to be — and harder than federal labor law says they should be.

My organization, the National Right to Work Legal Defense Foundation, has petitioned the National Labor Relations Board for a formal rulemaking to fix that — and a 2024 U.S. Supreme Court decision gives the board every reason to act.

In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the court ended decades of automatic deference to federal agencies’ expansive interpretations of the laws Congress wrote. Following Loper Bright , in July the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals struck down one such obstacle invented by the National Labor Relations Board to employee-requested decertification votes. With a third Trump appointee to the five-member board seated in August, the new majority doesn’t need to wait for courts to remove other such barriers.

The Trump board can and should promptly act on the rulemaking petition to enforce the text of the National Labor Relations Act and, in the process, defend workers’ free choice. Doing so would restore the Labor Board to its task of neutrally enforcing the law, rather than rigging the rules — as especially happened under the Biden and Obama Boards — to disenfranchise workers opposed to union affiliation.

Especially egregious are obstacles created by the National Labor Relations Board that automatically block workers’ petitions to hold decertification elections — no matter how large a majority of workers back them. These bars, which lack statutory justification, ignore the clear language of the law, which commands that the board “shall” conduct elections whenever a question of representation exists outside a one-year period following a previous election.

Our petition calls on the board to end what is known as the “successor bar” — struck down last month by the D.C. Circuit — which blocks votes after an employer changes ownership. But it also calls for rescinding other non-statutory obstacles to worker elections. For example, the “settlement bar” blocks a decertification vote when there is a National Labor Relations Board settlement to which the workers weren’t a party. The “contract bar” blocks a vote for up to three years after a union contract, no matter how dissatisfied the workers are with that contract. The “recognition bar” blocks secret-ballot decertification votes used to challenge unionization when it is imposed without an election through the abuse-prone “card check” procedure.

Our rulemaking petition also calls on the Board to overturn the Biden-era “blocking charge” policy that lets union officials block worker-requested votes by filing charges alleging misconduct by the employer, often without any evidence to back them up. These charges rarely have anything to do with the election, but they have the effect of preventing employee-requested votes from proceeding promptly.

A group of workers at Reed and Perrine Lawn Products in New Jersey saw the injustice of this policy up close when they sought to remove the United Food and Commercial Workers’ union from their workplace. Their majority-backed petition was filed in November 2024, but the union used abusive blocking charges to cling to power for another 18 months. When, in April of 2026, it was finally clear that union officials had no evidence to substantiate their blocking charges, and the vote became inevitable, union officials didn’t even bother to contest the vote.

Independent-minded workers face these tactics all too often — including in many cases where opposition to the union is unanimous in a given workplace.

The combination of artificial election bars, blocking charges and other policies has contributed to the reason why a recent study found 95 percent of currently unionized workers covered by the National Labor Relations Act have never even voted for the union that purports to represent them. That is why the rulemaking petition also requests the National Labor Relations Board effectuate the act by periodically requiring unions prove they have the support of a majority of employees.

Effective unions that workers voluntarily support have nothing to fear from these reforms. But for workers like those at Reed and Perrine — trapped for a year and a half by their own union because of dubious charges — these reforms could be the only way out.

This isn’t a fight between unions and employers, but a question of whether workers get a say in who represents them. The law already says what the Board must do: When workers petition for a vote, that vote must be held. The Trump board has the petition on its desk. After the Loper Bright decision, it has no excuse left to leave it there.

Mark Mix is president of National Right to Work Legal Defense.

articles.title: Van Hollen puts Schumer on notice
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Colom flips Mississippi in upset ▪ White House planning pushback ▪ Democrats regroup after Hegseth vote ▪ Huang facing more scrutiny Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is putting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on alert as he considers a possible bid for the top role in the upper chamber. The second-term…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is putting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on alert as he considers a possible bid for the top role in the upper chamber.

The second-term senator hasn’t said that he will run to become the majority leader in the next session of Congress, but his moves and comments have senators wondering if he’ll take a shot at the job.

Van Hollen was once seen as a future Speaker of the House when he represented Maryland in the lower chamber. His decision to leave the House and run for the Senate was then seen as a sign of the difficulty in moving up the Democratic House ranks during the era of Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

More recently, Van Hollen has openly discussed running for the White House in 2028. He’d be an underdog candidate in such a race, but it would give him more national prominence and could turn him into a Cabinet member if a Democrat were to win the Oval Office.

Whether Van Hollen challenges Schumer could be a matter of whether he thinks he’d have the votes to win a backroom vote among Democratic senators.

On Monday, Van Hollen told reporters Monday that he’s in “listening mode” on vying for the job.

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we’re going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” he said.

Comments he offered the following day were a bit sharper, as they targeted Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), the campaign arm of Senate Democrats.

The remarks specifically highlighted how some Democratic senators-elect, notably Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, won office despite the fact that Schumer and the DSCC supported other candidates in Democratic primaries.

“We have two newly elected senators who would not be there if Schumer and the DSCC had their way. Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee],” Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Ali Vitali .

Schumer has been a bit of a punching bag for the Democratic base, and particularly progressives, for years. On the cold open of the post-midterm election “Saturday Night Live,” Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) were parodied in a skit that suggested it would be better if both men stepped down from their positions.

But the reality is that Schumer likely has the support to win any contest on the leadership position within the Senate Democratic Caucus. He also had a strong midterm season, as Democrats have now gained eight seats in the Senate with the victory on Wednesday by Scott Colom in Mississippi. They are favored to win a ninth seat in Alaska, where Democrat Mary Peltola has a narrow edge on GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan .

But the unpopularity of Schumer with the base makes it not only easy for progressives to take shots at Schumer. It’s also an attractive thing to do.

El-Sayed told CNN last week that Van Hollen would be an “amazing” leader. El-Sayed has been singing Van Hollen’s praises for months, introducing him as the “next Senate majority leader” at a campaign rally in July.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) declared his support for Van Hollen, if he runs, in an interview with Jon Stewart on Tuesday, arguing that the Democratic Party needs “new leadership” to advance the party in a “much more vigorous way” to protect working families.

“We cannot have leadership in the Democratic Party who are going to do the same old, same old,” Sanders said.

Progressives aren’t the only ones who at least are interested in looking elsewhere from Schumer, who has led Democrats in the chamber since taking over for Harry Reid in 2017.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), a more moderate member, appeared at a press conference with Sanders on Tuesday in which both said they hoped for a competitive leader election . Slotkin said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen but declined to endorse him, saying she wants a concrete plan for governing from any candidate.

Democratic Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (Kan.) and James Talarico (Texas) have also withheld their support for Schumer, leaning into the push for generational change within the party.

Van Hollen has received more attention, particularly over the past year, during the second Trump administration.

He faced off with key members of the administration in April 2025 when he traveled to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia , a Maryland man who was wrongfully deported last year. Van Hollen was at first denied a meeting or phone call with Abrego Garcia but was later permitted to meet with him. He clashed with Secretary of State Marco Rubio during a congressional testimony the next month.

Van Hollen has also gained attention as among the harsher critics of Israel’s conduct during its war against Hamas and the U.S. relationship with its Middle Eastern ally. He’s been one of the relatively few senators to vote for resolutions from Sanders to place conditions on aid to Israel and block weapons sales , including just a few months into the war.

He introduced a resolution in September to direct the State Department to report on violence and human rights conditions in the West Bank, which narrowly failed mostly along party lines.

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports that Schumer is telling colleagues privately that he has already locked up the votes needed for him to become majority leader as he tries to snuff out any momentum for a challenger. Meanwhile, progressives are using the potential for a challenge to push Schumer to agree to a more ambitiously liberal agenda, including “Medicare for All.”

Senate Democrats told Bolton that Slotkin has also emerged as a possible contender, though she says she’s “not actively seeking” the role.

MISSISSIPPI DELTA: Democrat Scott Colom will flip Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith ‘s (R) seat in a major upset victory that further pads the incoming Democratic majority in the Senate.

Decision Desk HQ projected the race for Colom after a week of votes continuing to be counted after Election Day. Mississippi law allowed provisional and absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day to be accepted through Tuesday, and officials continued processing and counting those ballots Wednesday.

Hyde-Smith conceded her defeat to Colom in a video posted on social media Wednesday evening.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said the video. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Colom had tightened the gap behind Hyde-Smith on election night, and his lead only ticked up in the days that followed as more ballots were counted. He leads by about 4,500 votes, as of the latest tally.

Colom is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982. He also made history as the first Black person to be elected to the Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

INVESTIGATING THE INVESTIGATORS : The White House is signaling it intends to take an aggressive stance against efforts by the incoming Democratic-led Congress to investigate the Trump administration, warning that the way they wield their subpoena power “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

In a letter to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), White House counsel Will Scharf said any subpoena “ designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient” could be criminal, adding that “issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”

“Compulsory process is a power Congress has for oversight functions, and only for oversight functions ,” Scharf wrote in his letter to Garcia . “Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end.”

Democrats have discussed publicly their intention to investigate the Trump administration. Garcia, on the night of the election, issued a two-word statement, telling White House officials to “lawyer up.”

Garcia issued a defiant response yesterday, saying, “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” and asserting Congress’s authority to conduct oversight, which, he noted, “comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House.”

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse… We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ [Department of Justice] or from the President’s lawyers,” he wrote.

Punchbowl News was first to report on the letter yesterday, but Garcia’s spokesperson later noted that the Oversight Committee “has not received this letter yet.”

The Hill’s Mike Lillis and Sudiksha Kochi report that the issue is far from over, as a growing chorus of Democrats are now calling on the party to prioritize his impeachment when they take the gavel in January. ‘DIRTY TRICKS’ : House Democrats are up in arms after Republicans used a fast-track tactic to pass legislation intended to increase pay for disabled and injured veterans.

Democrats opposed the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act because they said it would expand some veterans benefits at the cost of slashing others. Leadership was whipping its members to vote no.

But when the Republican lawmaker presiding over the House brought the bill up for consideration, no Democrat demanded a recorded vote, a curious rarity that allowed it to be passed instantly by voice vote.

Democrats alleged that Republicans pulled Rep. Mark Takano (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Veterans Affairs Committee, away from the podium to discuss changes to the bill when the legislation was fast-tracked.

“On Veterans Day of all days, using dirty tricks to steal from Veterans is a disgrace,” a Democratic leadership aide said.

STANDING BY : The president is defending Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as the Big Tech leader and Trump ally is facing widespread scrutiny over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang has been in turmoil since a New York Times report that U.S. officials discovered Chinese business executive Alice Huang , who is not related to the Nvidia head, illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

The Nvidia CEO acknowledged that he was “unfaithful” to his wife and seemed to confirm the affair with Alice Huang. Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into the allegations.

But Trump has stood by Jensen Huang, calling him an “honorable guy.”

Adding to the controversy facing Huang, the Times reported Wednesday that he also had an extramarital affair with another executive at Nvidia. The Wall Street Journal reported later Wednesday that the company’s board is preparing to oust him.

Shares of Nvidia stock tanked early Wednesday evening following the second Times report.

The Hill’s Mallory Wilson and Miranda Nazzaro report that the situation raises questions about Trump’s close relationship with industry leaders and whether it could undermine their push for greater AI development in the U.S.

“I think the president’s impulse was to quell markets, and you know he’s not the one running any investigation,” said Ryan Fedasiuk , a senior fellow at Foundation for American Innovation.

articles.title: On the Ballot: Republicans started the redistricting war. Democrats may finish it
articles.summary: Republicans’ redistricting gambit backfired in the midterms as a Democratic tsunami swept the nation and flipped control on Capitol Hill, but the battle over congressional lines is far from over. The mid-decade redistricting wars that started in Texas last year roiled the midterm cycle as Republicans sought an edge and Democrats scrambled to counter the…
articles.body:
Republicans’ redistricting gambit backfired in the midterms as a Democratic tsunami swept the nation and flipped control on Capitol Hill, but the battle over congressional lines is far from over.

The mid-decade redistricting wars that started in Texas last year roiled the midterm cycle as Republicans sought an edge and Democrats scrambled to counter the would-be gains.

Against the backdrop of voter frustration with President Trump , the economy and the war in Iran, Republicans picked up just two of the 15 seats they targeted through redistricting as they lost the House majority, according to projections from Decision Desk HQ.

Now, boosted by their blue wave of wins, Democrats could be in position to redraw maps in their favor in more states for the cycles ahead — from Maryland, where voters passed an amendment that could pave the way for a redraw, to Wisconsin, where the incoming governor has pledged to sign a new map .

“What Texas unleashed is a declaration that there would be an all-out partisan war, and I think that has awoken the partisan warriors on the Democratic side,” said Justin Levitt , a professor at the Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who runs the All About Redistricting website.

“Republicans might not like what they started,” he added.

Bucking the typical every-10-years timeline for reshaping maps after the U.S. census, Republicans redrew congressional lines in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee this cycle, aiming to net more than a dozen seats in the House. Democrats pushed back with new maps in California and Virginia, and they gained a seat in Utah after a judge-ordered redraw — though Virginia’s voter-approved initiative was shot down by the courts.

Democrats then barreled through the midterms and performed well even in redistricted red states, climbing to what’s now expected to be a 259-176 majority in the House.

But even though Republicans lost and showed the limits of a partisan gerrymander, redistricting worked, experts say.

“Partisan gerrymandering acts largely as a seawall to constrain normal partisan tides, and a tsunami of turnout comes right up and over the top of that seawall,” said Levitt, who added that the redistricting was not a complete failure.

Nicholas Stephanopoulos , an election law professor at Harvard University Law School, echoed this view, arguing the GOP-led redraws “held up pretty darn well” in Florida and Texas.

“So in both those places, Republicans didn’t win the extra seats that they were dreaming of, but they largely avoided losses, even as the popular vote in those states moved by like 10 or 20 points against them.”

Now, as focus turns toward the next presidential race in 2028 and the next midterms in 2030, some states have already ruled out wading into the redistricting war any time soon.

In New Jersey, Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) said after the midterms she has no plans to redraw her state’s lines to help two newly elected Democrats stay in their Republican-leaning seats next cycle. Voters in Missouri, meanwhile, rejected a GOP-friendly House map for 2028 at the polls.

In Georgia, outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp (R) poured cold water on the idea of lame-duck redistricting before Democrats, including Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottom s (D), take power in January.

Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley (D) said last week he’d sign a redistricting bill if the incoming Democratic leaders got one through the state Legislature, where they flipped both chambers in the midterms.

In Maryland, voters this month approved a ballot measure that would make it easier for Maryland Democrats to pass a more favorable House map. Gov. Wes Moore (D), who just won a second term , has supported a redraw that would give Democrats all of the state’s eight congressional seats, but the state’s Senate president has so far blocked his party’s efforts.

New York has also positioned itself to redraw before 2028 through a constitutional amendment that state lawmakers weighed earlier this year.

Southern Democrats could also use their new leverage to try to pass new maps in North Carolina, Georgia or Texas, where the party won partial control of the state legislatures.

“I think the war that started by Trump before 2026 is going to keep on going,” Stephanopoulos said. “No one assumes we’re always going to have electoral environments like 2026, and so where Democrats have the power to redraw and it didn’t before 2026, I’m not sure having a favorable wave election this time should change their calculus going forward.”

Republicans could also try once more to regain their edge through redistricting in light of the 2026 electorate.

Red states in the South had gotten a green light from the Supreme Court’s landmark decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened a section of the Voting Rights Act and made it easier for states to redraw House districts without considering race.

But the GOP is in a “tougher boat” after the blue wave, Stephanopoulos said.

“They have a lot of uncertainty over what the electoral environment is going to be, and so I imagine some of them might be kind of gun-shy about redistricting, even if they thought they were going to do that before the election.”

Florida could consider another redraw, Levitt suggested, as Sunshine State Republicans “now know a lot more than they did before.” Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves (R) also previously signaled he expected state lawmakers to redraw maps before the state’s 2027 elections. And Indiana, where Trump’s redistricting push failed in 2025, could try again.

But even as lawmakers start looking at more potential line changes, debate rages on about possible reforms that could stem the redistricting tug-of-war.

Polls in recent years have shown broad voter opposition to partisan gerrymandering, though both sides appear more open to redistricting in response to aggressive changes across the aisle. Opponents say gerrymandering disadvantages voters and heightens political polarization.

“Redistricting wars will likely continue every year into the future if nothing is done,” the Brennan Center for Justice’s Michael Waldman wrote in analysis after the election.

“It seems quite likely Democrats will have control of Congress after 2028, and so if a Democratic candidate wins the presidency in 2028, I think high on the Democrats’ agenda is going to be all kinds of electoral reform,” Stephanopoulos said. “And that may very well include redistricting reform.”

The partisan redistricting war itself may be enough of a push for more policymakers to consider reforms.

“I think, I would hope, that folks have recognized that they’re not always going to be the ones holding the pen when it comes time to redrawing the lines,” Levitt said.

Welcome to The Hill’s On The Ballot. We’re Julia Mueller and Caroline Vakil — reach out to us on X ( @jmthewriter + @CarolineVakil) or via email ( jmueller@thehill.com + cvakil@thehill.com.)

An inside look at a Republican’s winning strategy in Maine

Paul LePage in Maine is poised to be the only Republican to flip a Democratic-held House seat this cycle. His campaign strategist Brent Littlefield pointed to one standout moment on the trail: the Republican’s nod to his French roots.

“Immigration built our nation,” LePage says in a 30-second ad from September, before saying in French, “I know, French was my first language in Lewiston.” He switches back to English, next saying, “But when people cross our border illegally, that’s wrong.”

The 30-second ad spot quickly went viral on social media, making “the point that we are a nation of immigrants, and we can acknowledge that we’re a nation of immigrants, but still be opposed to illegal immigration,” Littlefield said.

It also underscored LePage’s “unique background,” Littlefield said, noting that the two-time governor of Maine didn’t speak English until his pre-teen years.

It’s “a nod to the history and the tradition of the district, which has a dramatically large Franco background,” Littlefield added.

LePage is set to defeat Maine Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) for the House seat held by outgoing Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) — a rare Democrat to hold a reliably GOP-leaning district. Decision Desk HQ has not projected the race, which has entered ranked-choice voting, but Dunlap conceded to the Republican last week.

Littlefield credited LePage (“starts with the candidate”) for the campaign’s success in addition to a handful of other staffers and aides: Lauren LePage , the daughter of Paul LePage, and “a political force in her own right”; Elizabeth Gillen , who handled scheduling and operations; Damien LaRochelle and Michael Hersey, who both worked on the campaign’s finance efforts; Ryder Brewer and Andrew Baughman from the House Republicans’ campaign arm; and the media production team Cold Harbor Films.

Republicans have made religion a cornerstone of their politics, while Democrats struggled to find their own voice on matters of faith. But in the 2026 midterm elections, a crop of Democratic candidates sought to redefine that dynamic. Here’s more from The Hill’s Amie Parnes.

Democrat Scott Colom (D) extended his slim lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi by more than 3,000 votes. The Hill’s Ryan Mancini reports.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) says his party can “forget” about retaking the Senate majority in 2028 just a week after brutal losses for Republicans on deep-red turf, The Hill’s Ford McCracken reports.

As we turn to 2028, we’re asking folks in the elections space what they consumed on and off the 2026 campaign trail.

Brent Littlefield is a Republican political strategist who worked on Paul LePage’s House bid in Maine’s 2 nd District. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Most mornings I will read The Wall Street Journal, I read The New York Times, and I read The Washington Post. And then I get everything from Politico to read stuff in The Hill. I get Punchbowl News. I get Axios. All those newsletters — I read all those every morning, and then I start to read the clips and news stories from all of my different candidates with the different races I’m involved in all across the country. I read all those, and then I go back and for the elected officials I work with, who might not be up that cycle — and I still have a lot I work with on a day-to-day basis — I read all of their clips and all of their news from all of their states as well.

Cashews, peanuts, walnuts. Honey roasted peanuts. Any kind of nuts.

What album or podcast do you have on repeat?

Lately, I have been actually almost addicted to John Mayer for whatever reason and going back through his old and his new catalog, and I have no idea why. This has actually become my campaign soundtrack over the last three or four months, and literally picked a Spotify channel which was the best of John Mayer, and for whatever reason, I keep re-listening to it over and over and over again.

I have an espresso machine at home, and then if I’m on the road, I love to find a local coffee shop that’s unique to that area if I can find one, and then obviously default back to Starbucks if I can’t find one.

What TV show are you watching right now?

I have not had time to watch a TV show. I finally had time to go back and watch Ted Lasso, and I voraciously watched every single solitary episode of Ted Lasso.

I have gotten sucked into content creators on YouTube, and I love to watch travel shows on YouTube. And there’s a travel show with a British guy called Trek Trendy, and I’ve watched almost every single one of his travel episodes on YouTube.

The blue tsunami that wasn’t in South Dakota :

South Dakota offered a bright spot for the GOP last week after its midterm shellacking across the country.

Democrats had a lackluster night in the red stronghold, with Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Republican Sen. Mike Rounds easily cruising to victory. Democrats, for their part, did break a 18-year drought in the state after picking up four state legislative seats near Sioux Falls.

Still, Democrats did not make inroads like the party did in other solid red states, such as Texas and Iowa, this cycle.

David Wiltse, a political science professor at South Dakota State University and director of The South Dakota Polling Project, suggested the state largely bucked the national trends for a few reasons.

“The South Dakota electorate is pretty homogeneous, and they just don’t have these potential electorates that can be mobilized. We didn’t see a lot of shifts throughout most of white folks across the country,” Wiltse said. “We really saw those shifts in some of these electorates, again, Latinos and Black men.”

And unlike other agricultural-dominant states, such as Iowa and Kansas, Wiltse explained that South Dakota’s agricultural economy is more diversified and less susceptible to some of the same economic woes that have bedeviled farmers elsewhere.

“You have a lot of row crop farmers in the eastern part of the state who are hurt by this, but in the western part of the state, the ag economy is predominantly beef producers, and they are not as harmed by things like the tariffs and the rise in fertilizer and fuel prices,” Wiltse explained. “That’s not to say they’re not being pinched by it, but it’s just not as devastating for them as it would be your typical row crop farmer.”

Democrats also have a small bench of candidates to draw from, meaning that the party has often ceded what could be potentially competitive elections.

“One thing that the Democratic Party really struggles with in South Dakota is the candidate pipeline and getting quality candidates to decide to run,” Emily Wanless , an associate professor of government and international affairs at Augustana University in Sioux Falls said, describing it as a “chicken or the egg” dilemma.

articles.title: Absolute victory against Iran comes at a cost
articles.summary: Sunk-cost logic may drive White House strategy.
articles.body:
History shows that when leaders face political setbacks at home, they often seek to restore their standing through decisive action abroad. The temptation is to double down on an uncompromising foreign-policy objective rather than acknowledge failure or retreat. This quest can overshadow the strategic costs of achieving it.

President Trump faces such a moment with the unfinished war with Iran that he launched on February 28. Lacking a clear endgame, the war has proved costly and deeply unpopular at home and abroad.

Re-igniting or expanding the high-stakes conflict with Iran shortly after midterm election losses runs the risk of holding the already-reeling global economy hostage and further alienating a war-weary U.S. electorate concerned with economic stability and military overreach. The war was clearly a factor in Republicans’ loss of both chambers of Congress.

To salvage his image from the Iran war debacle, Trump, however, may reignite hostilities in the belief that his legacy hinges on compelling Iran to verifiably abandon its nuclear program. That includes low-level enrichment, which Tehran regards as its inalienable right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which allows peaceful nuclear-energy activities under International Atomic Energy Agency inspections.

Despite the recent electoral drubbing, Trump declared that he has no regrets about launching the war, even if American voters “weren’t happy with the oil price.” To make matters worse, there is intense internal friction within Trump’s national security team, with disagreeing advisers presenting him with starkly divergent risk assessments.

Advisers supporting escalation argue that unyielding military pressure is the only mechanism to compel Iran into total compliance. In this zero-compromise approach, stopping short of total victory renders the initial blood and treasure wasted.

Moderates, in contrast, caution that further strikes risk escalating into a broader regional confrontation, disrupting energy markets and locking the U.S. into an endless war. They also warn that Tehran can absorb immense punishment, resulting in a likely quagmire that would cloud the remainder of Trump’s term. Their prescription leans toward managed exits or off-ramps before political damage deepens further.

The blunt truth is that the Iran war has already proved to be one of the most strategically self-defeating wars in modern American history. It has weakened U.S. power, strengthened the very clerical regime it sought to overthrow, and handed geostrategic advantages to America’s principal global challenger, China. No less significant is the erosion in America’s international credibility and standing, even as the war has imposed significant economic costs on U.S. allies and partners (from Asia to Europe) by spiking energy prices and slowing growth.

The war already has fundamentally altered the strategic calculations of the Gulf monarchies, the central pillars of American power in the Middle East that today are pressing for de-escalation. These states, by prioritizing “Gulf First,” are no longer willing to blindly follow an “America First” administration. Any U.S.-initiated resumption of hostilities would only accelerate the rethink in the royal courts of the Gulf sheikhdoms.

Having already paid the domestic political costs of the Iran war, the White House has little incentive to accept an ambiguous draw. Indeed, Trump may want the conflict to end in a way that allows him to boast that launching it was worth the cost to the U.S. and the global economy.

The elevation of hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to chief of staff aligns with this logic. Miller’s public posture on the Iran campaign has framed the military campaign through an uncompromising lens (“not fighting with hands tied behind the back”).

To achieve a victory narrative dramatic enough to offset the political damage, the administration may seek to maximize coercive pressure through renewed hostilities to achieve Iran’s capitulation at the negotiating table or on the battlefield. However, if the Iranian regime were to give up its right to enrich uranium or admitted defeat under foreign duress, it could threaten its internal survival. If both sides view capitulation as politically costlier than continued conflict, escalation risks becoming self-sustaining.

Whether this leads to reignited hostilities depends on one key variable: whether the White House perceives the geopolitical and domestic backlash of renewed hostilities as lower than the political cost of an inconclusive outcome.

Trump is being forced to choose between two unpalatable options. He can cut the mounting losses — borne by the U.S., its allies and the global economy — and accept an inconclusive outcome, risking the narrative that launching the war was a major strategic error with no tangible payoff. Or he can double down on compellence, betting that an even tighter squeeze or further escalation can force Iran’s total capitulation on enrichment, thereby recasting the war as a historic victory.

With the U.S. again massing major forces near Iran, the sunk-cost logic may drive White House strategy. Once political capital is already spent, conservative conflict-management strategies give way to high-risk legacy moves. Forcing a complete, uncompromising outcome (“absolute victory”) carries massive strategic, economic and political trade-offs that may far outweigh any gains.

Absolute victory, in war as in politics, is often the costliest illusion. For the U.S., the choice is not between victory and retreat, but between an inconclusive peace and a deeper strategic defeat. A war launched to restore American strength must not end by further weakening America.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “Water: Asia’s New Battleground.”

articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign said Wednesday that Sen. The warning came after the latest batch of ballots showed the incumbent making only modest gains in a traditionally Republican stronghold. Peltola leads Sullivan by 3,975…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign said Wednesday that Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) is running out of opportunities to overcome her lead in the state’s closely contested Senate race.

The warning came after the latest batch of ballots showed the incumbent making only modest gains in a traditionally Republican stronghold.

Peltola leads Sullivan by 3,975 votes, down from 4,250 on Tuesday — largely from the conservative-leaning Mat-Su region — according to unofficial results released by the Alaska Division of Elections.

Sullivan gained just 275 votes on Peltola in the latest count, according to the Democrat’s campaign, a smaller margin than was anticipated from an area that has historically favored the GOP.

“As Mary continues to overperform in traditionally conservative areas around the state, today’s ballot drop is yet another proof point that Sullivan’s path to victory is non-existent,” Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement. “Voters are choosing Alaska first over party.”

“As we’ve said, tens of thousands of outstanding early votes and absentee ballots from Anchorage and rural Alaska remain uncounted and will break for Mary, sending her to the United States Senate,” Bruce continued.

As of Thursday morning, Peltola holds 48.57 percent of the vote to Sullivan’s 46.98 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Peltola’s lead has also fallen below the roughly 4,100 votes received by Dan J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot prompted the Trump administration to sue in October, arguing that voters could confuse him with the incumbent senator.

The Justice Department sought to block the certification of any election result affected by that confusion and asked a federal judge to segregate ballots cast for the similarly named candidate.

U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason tossed the lawsuit ahead of Election Day, ruling that the administration had failed to provide a workable plan to address its concerns without compromising voter secrecy or disrupting the election. The administration is appealing the decision.

Some also alleged that Peltola’s campaign sought out the other Sullivan to serve as a spoiler candidate , a claim the Senate candidate has denied. The controversy led to probes from federal officials and the state .

articles.title: Who got top scores on the polling report card for 2026?
articles.summary: Another election, another round of criticism directed at the polls. And that criticism, as always, is primarily from the losers.
articles.body:
Another election, another round of criticism directed at the polls. And that criticism, as always, is primarily from the losers.

The fact is, there are good polls and bad polls. In addition to the challenge of finding a random, representative sample, every pollster must make judgments on who is going to turn out. In close races, a few incorrect assumptions can lead to the wrong call.

Most critics — and, indeed, most people reporting on the polls — know next to nothing about proper survey research techniques, mathematics behind sampling, voter behavior or even what a poll really is. For the record, any poll ever conducted is a snapshot in time – what the population is thinking at that moment. The University of New Hampshire poll showing John Sununu (R) leading Senator-elect Chris Pappas (D) in early September was not necessarily wrong.

That fact is important when evaluating polling accuracy. In addition, there is always a small percentage of undecided voters, even on election eve. Those votes go somewhere. Even if the undecideds don’t show up (and many late undecideds don’t), the percentages for the candidates will go up. So, an accurate poll will understate the final percentage of both candidates.

Then there is the dreaded “margin of error.”

Simply put, all surveys attempt to estimate a larger population from a small (hopefully) representative sample. But it is an estimate. Normal margin of error is 2.5 to 4 points. The number reported in any poll is the best estimate. Erring by the top end of the margin of error is not good, and outside the margin of error is pretty bad. But a poll within 1 point is still a pretty good poll.

Where do undecided voters go? Mostly to the challenger or the party out of power. Essentially, voters know the incumbents and know their own circumstances. If they like the incumbents or are happy with their circumstances, they are already going with the status quo. It is an article of faith in campaigns that incumbents under 50 percent going into Election Day are at risk, regardless of their opponent’s polling.

Also, people don’t usually switch candidates unless given a strong reason to do so. The later in the campaign, the less likely they are to switch.

No poll gets it exactly right all the time. A poll could make a wrong call in a race but be more accurate than other polls. In the Mississippi Senate battle, where the final result appears likely to be a 49 percent to 49 percent Democratic victory, a late poll showing Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith leading Democrat Scott Colom 48 percent to 47 percent would be more accurate than one showing Colom leading 51 percent to 48 percent.

Good polls will show percentages that are below the final totals for both candidates, with a lower total for the challenger. Good polls should not overestimate candidates, at least not by more than 1 point. In my review, I used the summary data from RealClearPolitics . This data only incorporates pollsters who have been conducting polls over multiple cycles. Unlike other aggregator sites, RealClear has not been embarrassed by weak fly-by-night pollsters and outright frauds .

Overall, The New York Times and AtlasIntel were the best of the late polls. Emerson, Trafalgar, Rasmussen and Quantus had notable misses. But it is worth noting that Trafalgar had the best early poll of the whole cycle in South Carolina.

The New York Times and Atlas called every race correctly except South Carolina, where the Times had a 48-48 tie. Everybody else had Darline Graham (R) winning. But the late Times polls did not overestimate candidates in the key races, except in Michigan. The Michigan poll had Abdul El-Sayed at 53 percent (final: 52.5 percent) and Mike Rogers at 42 percent (final: 45.5 percent). I don’t think Rogers scooped up all the undecideds. Notably, they nailed Ken Paxton’s abysmal 43 percent in their final Texas poll. That is one race where I believe not a single undecided voter went for Paxton.

Much-lauded Atlas performed well in its directional calls. But accuracy was below the New York Times, because it overstated candidate percentages in a few races and in other races got the final percentages exactly correct. That would be fine for a projection, but not for a pre-election poll where, as I mentioned above, the estimate should lag the final total.

Polls that in the past have been what I would call Republican-friendly had notable misses. Rasmussen had Graham up 3 points in South Carolina and at 50 percent (final result: 51-47, to Annie Andrews), and in Iowa put Democrat Josh Turek over Republican Ashley Hinson by 1 point (final result: 51-46).

Trafalgar also missed on South Carolina but had Graham at 48 percent. It’s a reasonable miss, by perhaps 1 percent with the undecideds moving to the challenger. Trafalgar did have the best South Carolina poll, and I think one of the best early polls. Their Sept. 25 poll put Graham ahead only 43 percent to 42 percent. That poll correctly showed that Graham was in a lot of trouble, while other polls were giving her a 3-point to 5-point lead. I think Trafalgar accurately figured there were plenty of voters not sold on President Trump’s nepo-sibling pick .

The worst misses were by Emerson, which absurdly had Paxton over James Talarico by 2 points. The final result was a 12-point crush . Quantus had Paxton up by 1 point and Trafalgar had a tie. Emerson also fumbled Maine, putting incumbent Susan Collins ahead of Troy Jackson 51 to 49 percent. Jackson won 53-47 .

Everybody got Kansas right, and everyone whiffed on Minnesota, calling for Peggy Flanagan but overestimating Michele Tafoya.

The Big Chicken Award goes to Marist. In early polling, Marist gave the Democrats big margins in Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. While it is true that some of those numbers were likely overestimates, Marist was on to something — a big wave for the Democrats. Too bad Marist lost its nerve when everyone else’s polls showed tight races. My guess is that they tinkered with their turnout model and, as a result, their later polls herded their way closer to the rest of the industry.

Too bad. If they had stuck to their guns, they would be seen as oracles rather than just part of the crowd.

So, for 2026, The New York Times and AtlasIntel get the blue ribbons, Emerson gets the Price Is Right horn and Marist gets a chicken-salad sandwich. Enjoy.

Keith Naughton is a former campaign consultant and co-founder of the public affairs firm Silent Majority Strategies. Find him on his Substack, “Betting On Politics.”

articles.title: Himes urges Republicans to pass FISA during the lame-duck session
articles.summary: Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said Republicans would be wise to renew the nation’s warrantless spy powers during the lame-duck session. Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) allows the government to spy on foreigners located abroad, but privacy hawks on the left and right want…
articles.body:
Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said Republicans would be wise to renew the nation’s warrantless spy powers during the lame-duck session.

Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) allows the government to spy on foreigners located abroad, but privacy hawks on the left and right want to add a warrant requirement before agents can review information inadvertently collected on Americans.

Himes noted that is likely to be a growing contingent in the incoming Congress.

“I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck because it’s, you know, it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year, and, you know, I think they heard the message,” the lawmaker told The Hill.

“And I wasn’t even saying that’s good or bad. I’m just saying it’s a political reality that the 702 that gets reauthorized with a Democratic House and Senate is going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the lame-duck,” he continued.

“I just asked them to think about that because, you know, they’ve been screwing around,” Himes added. “The administration’s been screwing around and deprioritizing this issue, even though it’s, you know, exposing them to huge risk.”

The Republican-led House passed a bill to renew FISA 702 with limited reforms, but it has lingered in the Senate, which is working on its own bill but nonetheless allowed the powers to lapse over the summer.

Intelligence agencies have been operating under authority to run the searches given under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC), but the government risks that cell phone and communications companies won’t comply with requests once that authorization expires in March.

The FISA 702 battle does not split cleanly along partisan lines, and Himes and several other Democrats backed the GOP bill now waiting in the Senate.

A growing number of Democrats, however, argue that the U.S. must rein in spy powers — citing distrust of President Trump’s use of such a powerful intelligence tool as well as Americans’ privacy rights.

The GOP-led bill was passed without any provisions from Democrats, including language by Himes that would have required FISC review — though not a warrant — before reviewing any information collected on U.S. citizens.

articles.title: US attorney threatens Blumenthal with ‘significant legal consequences’ over ballroom probe
articles.summary: A top federal prosecutor warned Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) to preserve records related to his investigations into the donors funding President Trump’s White House ballroom project, accusing the senator of using congressional oversight to harass private citizens. Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, claimed in a letter dated Nov. 11…
articles.body:
A top federal prosecutor warned Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) to preserve records related to his investigations into the donors funding President Trump’s White House ballroom project, accusing the senator of using congressional oversight to harass private citizens.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, claimed in a letter dated Nov. 11 that Blumenthal’s probe threatened the constitutional rights of Americans who contributed to the roughly $400 million project. He warned that failing to preserve relevant documents could carry “significant legal consequences.”

In a post on the social platform X , Reitz accused the Connecticut Democrat of wielding Congress and his role on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations as a “weapon” against Americans for their political associations.

“I’m taking the first step to stop this abuse of power,” Reitz wrote.

Blumenthal responded to the demand to preserve records with a letter of his own addressed to Reitz, calling the implied threat of an investigation “baseless.”

“This investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Admin attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity,” Blumenthal wrote online .

The senator vowed that he “will not be intimidated” by the White House’s warning over the planned probes and said he would continue investigating what he described as the Trump administration’s misuse of taxpayer dollars and corporate involvement in corruption.

Blumenthal sent letters last month to more than a dozen previously undisclosed White House ballroom donors following a report from The Washington Post revealing their identities .

His office said the inquiries were part of an investigation into potential waste, fraud and abuse associated with the ballroom and other construction projects launched by the president across Washington.

articles.title: Senate Republican warns colleagues against downplaying midterm losses
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) is warning Senate Republican colleagues not to downplay the blowout Republican losses in last week’s election as “a normal midterm election loss,” saying they should instead work hard to win back voters who shifted to Democrats. “This was not a normal midterm election loss,” Kennedy told Fox News’s Sean Hannity in…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) is warning Senate Republican colleagues not to downplay the blowout Republican losses in last week’s election as “a normal midterm election loss,” saying they should instead work hard to win back voters who shifted to Democrats.

“This was not a normal midterm election loss,” Kennedy told Fox News’s Sean Hannity in an interview. “If you think that, congratulations, you’re stupid. As my friend Jim Justice says, Toby and Edith, they didn’t stay home. They voted for Democrats and we’ve got to get Toby and Edith back.”

Justice, the former governor of West Virginia, cites “Toby and Edith” as typical voters when talking about what his constituents want from their elected leaders.

Kennedy called for Republicans to work hard over the next 50-plus days to pass as much of President Trump’s agenda before turning over control of the Senate and House to Democrats.

“Here’s what we do — we’ve got 50-plus days while Republicans are still in charge,” he said, citing a permitting reform bill on the Senate floor, tax breaks for home sales, funding for the Defense Department and a stock-trading ban for members of Congress as priorities for the rest of the lame-duck session.

“Now those things are not going to solve all of Toby and Edith’s problems, but at least it’ll show Toby and Edith that we’re trying to do something,” Kennedy said.

Kennedy had urged Republicans to bring a budget reconciliation package to the Senate floor to circumvent a Democratic filibuster before the election, but other GOP senators objected to the idea because they didn’t want to take tough votes on amendments a few weeks before the election.

Kennedy told reporters in the Capitol on Wednesday that he wants to bring a budget reconciliation package to the floor before Christmas.

“I think we ought to get as close as we can to a consensus and we ought to try,” he said of bringing a budget reconciliation package to the floor in the lame-duck session, even though Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) indicated he’s not sure it has enough Republican support to advance.

Kennedy said the package could include language to raise the debt ceiling.

He said the legislation should primarily include funding for the Defense Department and a proposal sponsored by Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) to crack down on fraud that proponents believe could save hundreds of billions of dollars in taxpayer money.
