articles.title: A New Deal for the Age of AI: How Democrats can hold Big Tech accountable
articles.summary: The worst thing Democrats could do now is return to business as usual in Washington.
articles.body:
In 2018, House Democrats won 41 seats by hammering the message that Republicans, led by an unpopular president, gave sweetheart tax deals to a corrupt industry that hurt regular people. That year’s villain was the health insurance industry . This year’s was Big Tech — the first-ever election in which tech issues became a centerpiece of campaign ads.

The worst thing Democrats could do now is return to business as usual in Washington, just as voters handed them a tech accountability mandate. It would betray our campaign promises, fail to meet the moment, and create resentment in the electorate that will cost us in 2028.

Our mass condemnation of the tech industry has been swift. From 2020 to 2024, Democrats and allies ran just two ads that mentioned Big Tech. This year, more than 130 federal and statewide races ran on it, including 74 percent of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s Red to Blue races, 86 percent of Senate toss-ups and 100 percent of gubernatorial toss-up races.

According to some estimates, data centers were a core message of more than $170 million in ads . Candidates called for pauses on data centers , warned of AI’s dangers , and tied their Republican opponents to the industry in terms that previously would have been considered extreme. According to an SSRS exit poll, 56 percent of voters said that AI and data centers were crucial or a major factor affecting their vote.

Think about it: voters have watched tech giants write seven-figure checks to President Trump’s inauguration and political machine. Trump’s administration dropped federal investigations into the tech industry after it became the majority funder of the ballroom that Trump is building illegally adjacent to the White House. Big Tech got the tax breaks it long wanted, while millions of Americans saw their health care benefits slashed to pay for it while their energy bills skyrocketed .

No wonder, then, that in January , six in 10 voters told us the industry had too much influence in Washington, and by a two to one ratio believed the Trump administration was too cozy with Big Tech.

Meanwhile, Democrats’ advantage on handling AI’s impact grew from 8 points this summer to 12 in September ; Americans now trust Democrats more than Republicans on the most important issues to voters (health care and cost of living). AI and technology concerns shot up as well: Data scientist David Shor found AI rose in importance more in a single week this fall than in the entire previous year.

Tech is now central to affordability, as data centers drive up power bills and Big Tech companies use their market dominance to charge us more than our neighbors for the same products. It’s key for jobs and the economy, as chatbots and AI agents take over some work and transform the rest . It’s a rural issue and an environmental one, as these companies gobble up farmland for data centers, drain aquifers to cool them , and fire up new fossil fuel plants . And while all this happens, a handful of tech billionaires just keep getting richer on the backs of the people whose lives they are upending.

So here’s the strategy for Democrats over the next two years: govern like we campaigned.

Use the gavel to rein in the AI industry, expose Big Tech, force Republicans to choose between voters and their donors, and bring Big Tech’s CEOs before Congress and make them answer for their dangerous products and corrupt data center deals. Most importantly, build an agenda big enough to carry into 2028.

Let’s use our tech accountability mandate to pass a comprehensive social media, data privacy and AI safety bill that holds these companies responsible, bury the industry’s scheme to ban state AI laws, and write into law that Big Tech, not families, pays for its data centers . Make the companies profiting from AI pay their share, and use that money to rebuild what a decade of neglect and months of Elon Musk’s DOGE decimated.

Make sure the workers whose jobs AI is upending share in the wealth it creates, and generate new jobs with new public works projects. Harness AI for the public good — a technology sector that answers to citizens, not just shareholders. Then, make the industry that strained the grid help pay for the clean energy future.

Our party’s tech accountability mandate is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to show the American people that we can think big, be bold, and use the potential of AI to deliver a New Deal for the 21st century.

If we can make Big Tech answer to the public and ensure this technology serves all Americans, not just the billionaires who own it, we won’t just earn a coalition big enough to win the White House in 2028. We’ll have a movement built to last, a roadmap for unlocking our potential, and a future where our country is reaching for its highest heights.

Sacha Haworth is founder and CEO of the Tech Oversight Project. She is a veteran of Democratic campaigns all over the country, working for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, House Majority PAC, and on Capitol Hill.

articles.summary: Police say one person was killed and four others were wounded in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington, D.C., early Thursday morning, prompting a large police response and street closures in the nation’s capital. articles.body:
Police say one person was killed and four others were wounded in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington, D.C., early Thursday morning, prompting a large police response and street closures in the nation’s capital.

The shooter was also killed in the incident, a D.C. Metropolitan Police spokesperson told NewsNation. They declined to share further details about the shooter’s death.

The suspect had been barricaded inside his own unit at an apartment building near the scene at 15th and Q street, according to police. The suspect fired directly at officers while they attempted to negotiate with him. Police said the suspect suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound after negotiators established contact.

One of the four surviving victims is in critical condition. The victims were shot at multiple locations in the neighborhood, including inside a VIDA Fitness gym and across the street at a construction site. They were taken to different hospitals, where investigators have been able to interview some of them.

Police said the lone gunman, described as a white man, was armed with a handgun, though investigators have not determined whether he had additional weapons. Authorities believe he was a member of the VIDA Fitness Gym.

A shelter-in-place order was put in place for the areas surrounding Logan Circle and Dupont Circle, with instructions to go inside the nearest building and stay away from windows. That area of the city is just a short walk from the White House. The area includes multiple residences, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church and a Whole Foods supermarket.

The department’s Emergency Response Team was also deployed to the scene, and the FBI’s Washington Field Office is also assisting .

A witness inside the VIDA gym told a Washington Sun reporter that they heard a gunshot and saw a person on the ground inside the building. The witness said people fled the gym with their arms raised as police ordered them to clear the area.

VIDA Fitness temporarily closed its Logan Circle location following the shooting, and the facility will remain closed until further notice.

articles.title: Stephen Miller ‘should be preserving documents’: Garcia
articles.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Wednesday warned newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller that he “should be preserving documents,” as the incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee aims to launch sweeping probes into the Trump administration in the new Congress. Garcia, who already warned administration officials to “lawyer…
articles.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Wednesday warned newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller that he “should be preserving documents,” as the incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee aims to launch sweeping probes into the Trump administration in the new Congress.

Garcia, who already warned administration officials to “ lawyer up ” after Democrats made sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections, responded to CNN’s Kaitlan Collins when she asked if he thinks he can get Miller to testify.

“Well, look, we’re going to do everything we can to get him to answer questions,” he replied. “He certainly should be preserving documents, and I think what people need to realize is that if people thought that Donald Trump was somehow going to change his posture –– and that evaporated with the announcement of Stephen Miller.”

The California Democrat attributed Miller to being behind Trump’s deportation agenda, adding that the chief of staff “is not someone that should be leading anything in the White House, and it’s certainly someone that we have serious questions that we want answered.”

Collins asked Garcia about the responses from Trump, White House counsel Will Scharf and Attorney General Todd Blanche to the incoming House Oversight chair’s original warning, and what the likely fight next year will look like. The House Democrat said he thinks Trump is “clearly” hiding “something.”

“It’s a president that is cowardly, that doesn’t want to actually take the heat,” he continued. “For someone that gives so much anger and is so aggressive in his social media posts, he can’t take a few members of Congress demanding accountability and demanding for there to be actual responses.”

Garcia called it “comical how cowardly the actions of the administration have been” in recent days.

Scharf on Monday told Garcia via a letter that any probes opened by Democrats into the administration “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” He wrote that constant statements about “the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas … designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient,” claiming that “unlawful” subpoenas to deprive “citizens of their constitutional rights” could be met with their own investigations.

Garcia and other Democratic lawmakers took Scharf to task about the warning, with the incoming House Oversight chair telling reporters on Wednesday that it won’t “stop the important work.”

Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), another Oversight Democrat, told administration officials to “ come at me, bro .”

“So, we believe we have the right and we have been empowered expressly in the Constitution to make sure the president obeys the law,” Lynch told CNN’s Pamela Brown. “This is pretty basic, and so that’s the core function … and I speak on behalf of the chairman in this respect, I’m sure.”

articles.title: Congress should ban immigration officials from using social media
articles.summary: These posts are not law enforcement; they are shocking abuses of power.
articles.body:
A long running Immigration and Customs Enforcement practice is to post photos, on Instagram and other sites , of ICE detainees. Often, detainees are shown being put on an airplane for deportation.

In just the first year of the administration, at least 2,000 images were posted on X , and over 30,000 immigrants were listed on a new Department of Homeland Security website . Many of the social media posts also list criminal convictions — some erroneous — which are usually posted after a prison sentence has already been served.

Still others go further, mocking or disparaging immigrants based on their perceived ethnicity or national origin. In one image of a Sikh man posted shortly before the anniversary of 9/11, a caption read: “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive, Mr. Singh.” Just days after the Department of Homeland Security post was published, a young white man stabbed a Sikh truck driver in Wyoming.

As one Minnesota official said earlier this year about disparities regarding the number of ICE detainees being held in the state: “Despite our best efforts to correct the record and engage directly with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, they continue to publicly repeat information that is inaccurate and misleading.”

These posts are not law enforcement; they are shocking abuses of power.

The Department of Homeland Security’s communications endanger the individuals and institutions they vilify and mischaracterize the actual risks and benefits of migration. This directly contravenes this country’s obligations pursuant to its 1994 ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Elimination of all forms of Racial Discrimination, which cautions against portraying migrants as threats.

The U.N. also urges governments not to amplify myths, including those that equate migrants with disease, job theft, tax evasion or crime, or falsely suggest migrants disproportionately rely on public benefits.

The U.S. is an outlier in allowing its immigration enforcement agency to use social media accounts in this way. However, one key difference between the U.S. and other countries is that through its “ government speech doctrine ,” the Supreme Court interprets the First Amendment to give the government wide latitude to engage in all kinds of expression, including xenophobic speech.

But the fact that Homeland Security can engage in such speech does not serve as sufficient justification. The key question for every government agency should be whether the law enforcement and public safety value gained from a particular communication outweighs the invasion of privacy or dignity that is compromised when posts are published.

This principle is not novel nor impractical. It is a simple balancing test that can be applied by officials using regulatory guidelines and ensured through judicial review.

Indeed, the U.S. Marshals Service has already recognized this very concern for more than a decade. Its policy states : “Once a prisoner has been arrested, the general rule is that no release should be made, because release of photographs of that prisoner to the media or public would not serve law enforcement purposes.”

The same reasoning applies to ICE detainees. Once a person is in custody, publicizing their image serves no apparent law enforcement purpose. American governments must wield the awesome power of speech responsibly and only for legitimate public purposes.

Since the United States does not have constitutional law guardrails that control this pernicious form of government speech, Congress must step in by establishing clear statutory limits on when and why Homeland Security may publicly release images of people in immigration detention.

In the meantime, given the ongoing invasions of privacy and dignity these accounts represent, Homeland Security’s social media accounts should be suspended unless and until the agency demonstrates that it can use social media responsibly.

Beth Lyon is a clinical professor of Law at Cornell University, where she co-directs the Migration and Human Rights Program and serves as affiliated faculty to the Cornell Center on Democracy .

articles.body:
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) apologized for missing a vote that would have put the House closer to impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“Well, it is Wednesday, and I am here just off of the House floor. Our colleagues are struggling once again to pass another terrible bill, and I wanted to take a moment during the recess to just talk about what happened last night, to talk about the motion that was on the floor and to explain what happened,” Stansbury said in a video posted to Facebook on Wednesday.

“Let me start by saying, I am so sorry. There is no one who is more disappointed in myself than me that I was not here that the moment that gavel dropped, as the Republicans were trying to bury this impeachment of Pete Hegseth,” the New Mexico Democrat added.

On Tuesday, Stansbury said she and other lawmakers could not make it to the Capitol in time to vote against an effort from Republicans to stop the impeachment of Hegseth due to a traffic incident and a police escort.

“Like other Members of Congress, Rep. Stansbury was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due [to] a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote,” her office said in a statement on the social platform X. “When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out.”

According to Stansbury, she got to the House chamber shortly after lawmakers voted 211-204 to refer the measure against Hegseth to committee, effectively shelving the effort until next year, when Democrats take over both chambers of Congress.

“She immediately filed a report of her vote of ‘NO’ to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record,” her statement continued. “Pete Hegseth must be impeached now.”

articles.body:
The Hill this November is again focusing on lifting veterans’ voices and spotlighting the policy issues that impact more than 15 million U.S. veterans.

This year, that includes the much-needed access to dental care that remains out of reach for nearly 3 in 4 veterans who do not qualify for Veterans Affairs’ dental coverage. For those who do qualify, provider shortages, geographic barriers and costs can still make obtaining care difficult, particularly in rural communities.

The consequences can extend beyond oral health. Veterans experience high rates of chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes, and research from CareQuest Institute and the American Institute of Dental Public Health estimates that treating gum disease among just 25 percent of veterans could result in nearly $3 billion in annual savings associated with treatment for those conditions.

How can policymakers expand access to dental care for veterans while addressing provider shortages and geographic barriers? What role can community providers, innovative care models and public-private partnerships play in reaching veterans, particularly those in rural and underserved areas? And how can improving preventive oral health care contribute to better health outcomes while potentially reducing broader healthcare costs?

Join us on Nov. 12, for The Hill Talks: Strengthening Dental Care for Veterans, a virtual event featuring a forward-looking discussion with lawmakers, veterans’ advocates, oral health experts and healthcare leaders to examine the barriers veterans face in accessing dental care and the policies and partnerships that could shape the future of veterans’ oral health.

articles.title: The Jensen Huang affair exposes corporate America’s China problem
articles.summary: China has used its intelligence services, business relationships and industrial policies to obtain American technology and commercial secrets for decades.
articles.body:
The revelation that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative has sent shock waves through the world of business and politics. Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation, and the FBI is reportedly examining the matter.

But the implications go far beyond one executive’s personal conduct.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are at the center of the global artificial intelligence competition, and China has been working aggressively to acquire the technology, which Washington has sought to keep out of its hands . Huang is a key figure in the technological competition between the world’s two most powerful countries, with direct access to President Trump and considerable influence over American technology policy.

The New York Times reports that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about Jensen Huang. She was an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that was accused of sending chips to China despite export restrictions. China denies the espionage allegations, and Nvidia has disputed suggestions that its dealings compromised sensitive information.

What makes this story especially troubling is the range of intelligence that could be obtained through such a relationship. Espionage is not simply about stealing classified documents or proprietary technology. A conversation about what President Trump said privately concerning China, an observation about disagreements within his administration or advanced knowledge of Nvidia’s negotiating positions could be enormously valuable to Beijing.

And that information need not be deliberately disclosed. Intelligence officers are trained to develop relationships, cultivate trust and elicit information that their targets might not even recognize as sensitive.

The alleged operation bears the hallmarks of the “honeypot,” in which romantic or sexual relationships are exploited for intelligence purposes. China has a history of such operations against American targets. Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, cultivated relationships with American politicians, including former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), and also reportedly had intimate relationships with two Midwestern mayors.

There is an important distinction between Chinese intelligence services and their American counterparts. Unlike Chinese intelligence officers, American case officers are prohibited from using sexual relationships or blackmail to recruit and manipulate intelligence targets. U.S. officers undergo extensive security vetting, including polygraph examinations, and can face serious disciplinary consequences for violating these restrictions. Chinese intelligence services, by contrast, have demonstrated a willingness to use seduction and coercion to obtain information and influence their targets.

For those of us who conduct corporate investigations, the broader pattern is familiar. China has used its intelligence services, business relationships and industrial policies to obtain American technology and commercial secrets for decades.

During the late 2000s and much of the 2010s, foreign companies entering certain Chinese industries faced joint venture requirements that could expose valuable intellectual property to local partners. Our investigations helped American companies understand how inadequate due diligence on executives appointed by Chinese partners left them vulnerable to intellectual property theft.

There have been enormous consequences. Sinovel, a major Chinese wind turbine manufacturer, recruited an employee of American Superconductor who helped it obtain proprietary software and source code. A federal court found that the American company suffered more than $550 million in losses.

But the Huang affair illustrates an even more consequential vulnerability. America’s top executives increasingly occupy positions of national security significance without having the training or protection afforded to government officials.

Huang’s conversations with senior policymakers, his knowledge of the global semiconductor industry and his ability to influence decisions about advanced technology make him an extraordinarily valuable intelligence target. The same is true of executives in artificial intelligence, aerospace, defense, biotechnology and other industries critical to American national security.

Corporate security programs must evolve accordingly. Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks and responding to physical threats. Those responsibilities remain essential, but they are no longer sufficient.

Security teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts. Executive protection must include counterintelligence awareness, not simply physical security. Boards and senior management should understand that a company’s greatest vulnerabilities may involve people rather than technology.

Washington is also reconsidering its approach. Former CIA Deputy Director David Cohen has argued that American intelligence should be more willing to collect and share economic intelligence that could benefit U.S. companies. Meanwhile, The Washington Post recently reported that the Pentagon is considering a clandestine program focused on China, potentially deploying intelligence officers posing as businesspeople to gather economic intelligence.

Such initiatives may help the United States compete more aggressively with Chinese espionage. The CIA has already devoted substantial resources to the challenge. By early 2025, approximately 20 percent of its budget was focused on China-related intelligence activities. But even as Washington develops new offensive intelligence capabilities, American companies must recognize that they are already on the front lines of this struggle.

Whatever the Nvidia investigation ultimately reveals, the broader warning is unmistakable: America’s corporate leaders have become national security targets and protecting them must become a national security priority.

Don Aviv, CPP, PSP, PCI, is CEO of Interfor International . Jeremy Hurewitz is a former Shanghai-based journalist, head of Interfor Academy, and author of “ Sell Like a Spy .”

articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday expressed dissatisfaction with the way the Republican Senate worked, calling its moves “devastating” to the GOP and saying they led to the party’s colossal losses in the midterm elections.

“The Republican Senate can no longer be the place ‘where things are sent to die.’ Not passing THE SAVE AMERICA ACT (Voter I.D., Proof of Citizenship), sent up five times by the House, was devastating to the Republican Party in the Midterms,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

“Not terminating the Filibuster, and getting EVERYTHING even ‘dreamt’ of, approved, when the Dems will definitely do so, will go down as being one of the greatest mistakes in the Political History of America,” he added.

The midterms were swept up by a “ blue wave ,” with Democrats securing historic wins across the nation, flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states such as Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Maine and Iowa, among others. The Democratic Party is set to take control of both the House and Senate in January.

Up until Wednesday, the Democrats were set to hold 54 Senate seats, but with Democrat Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi’s competitive Senate race , the party will now hold 55 seats. They could potentially pick up Alaska, too, in a tight race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R). She holds a slight lead over the Republican after the latest vote drop .

The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, referenced by the president in his post, would have tightened identity requirements for voter registration by asking for proof of U.S. citizenship to vote in federal elections. The bill passed the House but did not clear the Senate .

In the weeks leading up to Election Day, the administration escalated its efforts to stop noncitizens from voting in the midterms, with states such as California and Washington coming under federal scrutiny for potentially having noncitizen voters on their respective voter rolls. Federal law indicates that only U.S. citizens are permitted to vote in federal elections, according to a fact sheet from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The president, in his post, also congratulated Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.), who won reelection to serve another term as Senate Republican leader on Tuesday. In the lower chamber, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their conference in the next Congress.

articles.title: Winning elections won’t save abortion access
articles.summary: These Democrats won with our pro-choice votes. Now that they are in power, it’s time to put power into action without delay.
articles.body:
In the years after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade , voters in 17 states have weighed in on abortion-related ballot initiatives, with the abortion-rights side winning in 14 of them , including Kansas, Kentucky and Ohio. This election year, midterm voters in three additional states — Missouri, Nevada and Virginia — approved ballot measures that will protect abortion rights. Idaho voters rejected a similar measure .

At the state level, candidates who support abortion rights won Democratic trifectas in six key states and establishing control of a majority of state legislatures for the first time in more than 15 years . In addition, Democrats now control 28 , possibly 29 governorships and have flipped five state attorneys general offices , including that of Texas. Congress will now be dominated by a solid Democratic majority, ushering in solid support for legal abortion.

Too many of these candidates avoided the word “abortion” on the campaign trail because they did not view it as a winning issue. Voters proved the skeptics wrong yet again.

On paper, the political case for restoring reproductive freedom has never been stronger. But winning Democratic seats alone won’t restore our rights.

Since Dobbs, the fight over abortion has centered on access to a single pill, mifepristone , which has been used safely in the U.S. for more than 25 years for abortion and miscarriage management. Medication abortion, typically a regimen that begins with mifepristone, accounted for 64 percent of clinician-provided abortions in 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute. By 2025, telehealth abortion, which depends heavily on mifepristone, accounted for 27 percent of U.S. abortions, according to the Society of Family Planning.

Hundreds of thousands of women each year now depend on that pill, and the laws that protect access to it. With escalating anti-abortion attacks on mifepristone access , we need elected officials to enact and defend laws to keep it available.

Eight states enacted telemedicine abortion shield laws after Dobbs . These laws protect clinicians and other supporters who provide care by telehealth from shield states to patients wherever they live. Telemedicine abortion gives patients an option when travel is too expensive or difficult because of work, school or child care commitments. Because of telemedicine, the number of abortions in America has held steady at about 1.1 million in 2025, even as clinics closed across states with bans.

Telemedicine abortion shield laws have held up against anti-abortion attacks. When Louisiana sought to extradite a California doctor in January, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) invoked the shield law and refused . When Texas obtained a default judgment of more than $100,000 against a New York doctor, a court clerk refused to enter it, and a judge upheld that refusal , both citing New York’s shield law.

Abortion opponents are well aware of the power of telemedicine to ensure access to abortion, and have worked relentlessly to undermine it. Last May, in a lawsuit brought by the state of Louisiana, a federal appeals court reinstated a nationwide requirement that mifepristone only be available if dispensed to a patient appearing in-person. Fortunately a Supreme Court stay has kept mail delivery available while the case continues .

Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the FDA ordered an unnecessary safety review of mifepristone , to be released in March 2027, even though the drug has a 25-year global safety record. Dr. Heidi Overton, the president’s nominee to run the FDA, was dodgy at her confirmation hearing, but her record is clear: She once called the agency’s decision to allow mail delivery “chemical abortion on demand.”

The next escalation came in September, when the attorneys general of Louisiana, Alabama and Arkansas asked the Supreme Court to hear their lawsuit against New York, California and Massachusetts, seeking to invalidate those states’ shield laws . The same attorneys general then filed a separate federal suit against 30 alleged telemedicine providers and supporters . If either case succeeds, abortion access could decrease nationwide. Not satisfied with banning abortion in their own states, these elected officials are spending significant state resources to override other states’ laws.

The majority of U.S. voters are pro-choice on abortion, and they have firmly and frequently rejected such attempts to ban it. The Democrats we elected must push back now.

Senators can reject Overton’s nomination and demand that the FDA show the evidence behind its review before it acts. When President Trump seeks Senate confirmation for his administration or Supreme Court justices over the next two years, Democrats must ensure they support abortion rights.

Attorneys general, who play a key role in enforcing abortion laws, can defend shield laws in court and join the mifepristone cases on the side of patients. Governors and legislators can protect clinicians who prescribe mifepristone, even if the FDA meddles with the science of its safety. New York has a law supporting mifepristone access that would do that. It has passed both chambers and awaits Gov. Kathy Hochul’s (D) signature .

New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland had shield legislation pending last session, and states that are newly Democratic trifectas — Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Arizona — likely have the votes to act similarly. California can reinforce its commitment to refuse to extradite abortion providers by passing a bill that Newsom wrongly vetoed last September; now Governor-elect Xavier Becerra (D) has the chance to support our rights by signing it as soon as it reaches his desk next session.

These Democrats won with our pro-choice votes. Now that they are in power, it is time to take action without delay.

Julie F. Kay, a human rights attorney, is the founder and CEO of Reproductive Futures and co-author of “Controlling Women: What We Must Do Now to Save Reproductive Freedom.“

articles.title: Veteran suing over Trump arch: ‘We continue to be gaslighted’
articles.summary: One of the Vietnam War veterans suing to block construction of President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch reiterated his criticism of the project on Wednesday, after the president said the structure would be dedicated to U.S. veterans. “We continue to be gaslighted by him and the administration,” Michael Lemmon told CNN’s Erin Burnett. “Nobody believes, frankly,…
articles.body:
One of the Vietnam War veterans suing to block construction of President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch reiterated his criticism of the project on Wednesday, after the president said the structure would be dedicated to U.S. veterans.

“We continue to be gaslighted by him and the administration,” Michael Lemmon told CNN’s Erin Burnett. “Nobody believes, frankly, anything he says anymore. It has no credibility. We can all see through it. Each new excuse that comes up is just designed to move his personal vanity project over.”

Lemmon filed a temporary restraining order request with two other veterans and an architectural historian in September, after lodging an initial complaint in February arguing the project does not have the required congressional approval. Washington, D.C., and Virginia also sued to block the arch’s construction at the end of October.

During a Veterans Day event on Wednesday at Arlington National Cemetery, Trump said the arch would be dedicated to “our great veterans and our great militaries,” claiming these groups have been “waiting for it for 200 years.”

Lemmon pushed back on the president’s words in his CNN interview later that evening, calling the proposed arch “disrespectful to veterans.”

“We have been disrespected and disregarded, the Vietnam vets in particular, for some 60 years now,” he told Burnett. “And to have this person, who has been reputably reported to have called us ‘suckers and losers’ for serving, pretend … that this is somehow dedicated to us, I don’t know anyone who buys that story.”

The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 last week to approve plans to build the arch, despite hearing hours of public testimony opposing the project.

Critics of the construction proposal have pointed to safety concerns with its potential impact on D.C. airspace, while others have called it an insult to the service members who are buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

The arch would be constructed on the border between D.C. and Virginia, and a past proposal incorporated military plans , with the president saying the structure could be used for snipers and drones. The final plans approved by the NCPC did not include the military complex.

articles.title: More than half of Republicans prefer 2028 nominee to take different approach from Trump: Poll

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll, 52 percent of Republican or Republican-leaning respondents said they want a 2028 GOP nominee with “a different approach to governing as Donald Trump.” Forty-six percent of…
articles.body:
More than half of surveyed Republicans are looking for a 2028 presidential nominee with a different approach from President Trump, according to a new poll.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll , 52 percent of Republican or Republican-leaning respondents said they want a 2028 GOP nominee with “a different approach to governing as Donald Trump.” Forty-six percent of the same group said they want a nominee with “a similar approach to governing as Donald Trump.” Two percent skipped the question.

The poll took place between Friday and Monday, shortly after this year’s midterms. Republicans faced blowout defeats in the elections, losing in places where Democrats have historically had disadvantages like Kansas and Texas.

During this year’s election cycle, Republicans faced an uphill battle due to the unpopular Iran war, Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 37.7 percent on Thursday morning , while his disapproval rating was at 60 percent.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll, 46 percent of respondents said Democrats securing both the House and Senate in the midterms was “a good thing,” while 29 percent called it “a bad thing” and 24 percent were “not sure.” Two percent did not answer the question.

On Thursday , Trump voiced displeasure with the work of Senate Republicans, referring to their moves as “devastating” for the party and claiming they resulted in the GOP’s significant losses in the midterm elections.

“The Republican Senate can no longer be the place ‘where things are sent to die.’ Not passing THE SAVE AMERICA ACT (Voter I.D., Proof of Citizenship), sent up five times by the House, was devastating to the Republican Party in the Midterms,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll featured 1,705 respondents and a margin of error of 2.4 percentage points.

articles.title: Want to be president? Look to the states
articles.summary: Whatever that president has, and whatever that president wants, it goes through the states.
articles.body:
The midterms are over, and the race for the Democratic presidential nomination has begun. Before the first candidate books a flight to South Carolina, Nevada or — if they’re smart — to Virginia, there is a little they can learn from state capitols like Richmond.

If you want to win, govern and rebuild the Democratic Party, look at state governments, and come up with a plan to work with us.

Tip O’Neill was credited with saying “ all politics is local .” It still is. Somewhere along the way, our party forgot that. Republicans never did.

When Barack Obama came into office, the experts said demographics were destiny and the Republican Party was headed for a generation in the wilderness. Republicans set out to show that wasn’t true, and they didn’t start in Washington. Through the American Legislative Exchange Council , Project RedMap and other organizations most voters have never heard of, they went to work in the states, one legislature at a time.

They took over state governments. They converted white working-class voters, and later a growing share of Latino voters, to the Republican brand. They redrew the maps. Democrats lost more than 900 state legislative seats during those eight years, and Republicans built the dominant position in driving the national narrative that they hold today.

Republicans didn’t take back the country from Washington. They took it back from Columbus, Raleigh and Austin, one statehouse at a time — and Washington followed.

Virginia Democrats learned the same lesson the hard way. We won the House of Delegates in 2019 on a wave of opposition to President Trump, but then we promptly lost it in 2021 . We had acted too much like our colleagues in Congress — delivering small victories for activists in our base while avoiding the hardest issues that most Virginians cared about.

So we got back to work. In 2023, we were running with a Democratic president whose approval ratings were historically low and against a popular Republican governor who poured millions into beating us. We held the state Senate . And in the House of Delegates, the most local of local races, we picked up three seats and flipped the chamber .

We won because our candidates focused on what is important to the everyday American: what groceries and rent cost, whether the schools are good, whether the neighborhood is safe.

For two years, the legislature tried mightily to pass bills to deliver on our promises, but Gov. Glenn Youngkin (R) blocked us at every turn. So, in 2025, Virginians gave us 64 of 100 seats , our largest majority in more than three decades, and a Democratic governor to work with.

Then we governed. We put the minimum wage on a path to $15 an hour . We made Virginia the first state in the South with paid family and medical leave . We created the first in-the-nation data-center consumption tax . We guaranteed paid sick days to more than a million workers who had none. And this fall, because of the votes we took, Virginians could decide whether to write abortion, marriage equality and voting rights into our constitution.

Winning locally lets you produce actual results for actual people. National Democrats should get in on the action, and fast. You can’t count on Trump to be the force that carries you. He will not be on the ballot in 2028. Whoever wants to lead this party will need more than a villain. They will need a record and a plan. Right now, the best records in this party are being built in state capitals. So are the only plans with a credible chance of making a difference in people’s lives.

So here is what I want every candidate to understand before this campaign starts. The next president has to recognize how important the states are. Whatever that president has, and whatever that president wants, it goes through the states. States run the elections. States draw the congressional maps. States run Medicaid, fund the schools and pave the roads. States will protect people’s rights, or strip them. States will fix the government so it works for people, or let it rot.

When Trump wanted more Republican seats in Congress, he didn’t ask Congress. He turned to the Texas Legislature . When Virginians needed paid leave, we didn’t call Washington, D.C. We made it happen.

That is how the founders intended it. Our system is more than three branches in Washington stuck in an endless doom loop of partisan stalemate. It is federalism, with meaningful power retained by states that are still wielding it in ways big and small. Justice Brandeis gave us the idea of states as laboratories of democracy.

Democratic power can only be maintained if national leaders partner with the states. That means investing in legislative races every year, including the years when no one is running for president. It means treating state legislators as partners in governing, especially when Congress refuses.

Washington is where Democratic ideas go to get debated. The states are where they go to get done. Anyone who wants to be president should start there.

Don Scott (D), who represents Virginia’s 88th District, is the 58th Speaker — and the first Black Speaker — of the Virginia House of Delegates .

articles.title: P’nut the squirrel’s former owner has been detained by ICE and may be deported
articles.summary: The arrest was the latest twist in the tale of Peanut, also known as P’nut, a once-orphaned squirrel whose fun antics made him a social media star.
articles.body:
PINE CITY, N.Y. (AP) — When New York wildlife officers euthanized a couple’s pet squirrel Peanut two years ago, Republicans including Vice President Vance seized on the critter’s killing as just another example of government overreach from meddling Democrats.

“The same government that doesn’t care about hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrant criminals coming into our country doesn’t want us to have pets. It’s the craziest, the craziest thing,” Vance said at a rally just before the 2024 election.

Now, President Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has put one of the late squirrel’s owners in an immigration jail, pending possible deportation to Germany.

Daniela Bittner was arrested by immigration officers in mid-October at a small airport near New York’s border with Pennsylvania. DHS issued a statement saying Bittner was arrested because she “chose to overstay her welcome in defiance of our nation’s laws.”

Since then, Bittner has been moved through multiple immigration lockups and is now housed in Texas, according to her husband, Mark Longo — who called conditions in the lockups “deplorable.” He blamed her detention on an immigration paperwork mix-up.

“They put Peanut on a pedestal, won their election, and threw him off that pedestal immediately,” Longo said.

The arrest was the latest twist in the tale of Peanut, also known as P’nut , a once-orphaned squirrel whose fun antics made him a social media star. That is, until state officials got multiple complaints that the couple were illegally keeping wild animals in their house as pets, including the squirrel and a racoon.

During one inspection, Peanut bit the gloved thumb of a wildlife biologist and was euthanized so the squirrel could be tested for rabies.

News stories about the episode earned the family sympathy and caught the attention of Republicans on the campaign trail, who criticized the state’s response and New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul.

Longo said he tries to steer clear of politics, but that he can’t help but feel like the government keeps wading into his life.

“I’m begging the world to find an answer as to why this keeps happening to me,” he told The Associated Press by phone Wednesday. “One time, you can call it what it is. Two times, it’s now becoming a little bit more of a target.”

Longo said he and Bittner made a mistake on one of her immigration forms and didn’t catch the error while they were dealing with the dustup over Peanut’s seizure and killing.

“You know, arrest the people who deserve to be arrested. My wife is not one of them,” he said.

“You’re telling me, all of this because my wife and I forgot to do the proper form?” he added.

Longo said local officials have been looking into his wife’s case and that he’s spoken about her arrest to UFC chief Dana White, a longstanding ally of President Trump whom Longo said he met after Peanut was taken.

The squirrel’s former owner said he will have to shut down the animal sanctuary he and his wife run if she is deported.

“The only outcome that will save this place is my wife not being deported,” Longo added.

articles.title: Election results may portend new directions
articles.summary: Following a midterm election that saw significant Democratic gains, the 119th Congress returned to work amidst a divided government and skepticism regarding future bipartisan cooperation.
articles.body:
This week, the House and Senate returned to work after a five-week hiatus for the midterm elections. Physically, the 119th Congress still sits in the District of Columbia. Emotionally, it lies in a state of shock after being engulfed by a blue tsunami, in which Democrats flipped a projected 44 Republican seats in the House and, so far, seven in the Senate, with two results outstanding.

With only 20 legislative days left in this final session, Congress has a full plate of work to complete if it wants to leave town with some modicum of respect still intact. Simultaneously, Capitol Hill is crowded, not so much with tourists, but with nearly 120 new House members — one-fourth of the chamber’s membership, who are here for a 10-day “ New Member Orientation .”

Given that there were 74 open seats left by 42 Republican members and 32 Democrats who either died, retired, were defeated in primaries or ran for other office, it has been a somewhat hectic week in which the freshmen have been learning the ropes: drawing by lot for their new offices and sitting through lectures on everything from hiring Capitol and district office staff, to the House ethics code, to introducing bills and participating in committee and floor deliberations.

Meantime, the outgoing members will not only be casting their final votes and drawing their final paychecks next month, but have been given orders on when to vacate their offices to make way for the new class in town.

It is ironic and downright weird that on election eve President Trump chose the base of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool as the venue for his closing campaign remarks, claiming it was a fitting example of fulfilling his pledge to “fix Washington.”

Never mind that the memorial pool had become a blue lagoon of executive mismanagement and ineptitude, given its flaking blue bottom and algae-filled waters. The president persisted in insisting the damage had been caused by vandals, even though scientific investigations concluded it had been the result of shoddy workmanship.

The reflecting pool repair project has itself become a scandal of a thousand self-inflicted cuts leading back to the White House and no-bid contracts with golf club swimming pool repair guys. Moreover, last week’s Washington Post reported there are new cracks appearing on what is now a two-tone-blue pool. The shellacking of the pool’s bottom in American flag blue did not overshadow the big blue shellacking the president’s party took at the polls.

This leads to the question of how the two parties, with split control between the Congress and White House, will govern over the next two years. The optimistic slant is that there will be a “reckoning.” Yet, neither party seems to have a game plan as to how to govern the country given the new division of powers. Instead, both parties seem stuck in the same old rut of blaming the other for mounting problems. The president’s elevation last week of combative hardliner Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff seems to reinforce the fear there will be more of a wrecking than a reckoning.

They say there are two kinds of politicians: the show horses and the work horses. Today, the show horses of both parties circle the ring aimlessly, while the work horses stand idly by, having voluntarily ceded much of their constitutional authority to the president and his Cabinet. Both show horses and work horses yearn to return to their chosen roles of political messaging and deliberative lawmaking, respectively. However, Congress will likely remain thwarted for the last two years of the president’s term.

Opinion polls taken before the election indicate the public wants something totally different from what Washington has been doling out. At least on questions about whether the parties should do more to work together to solve the problems that make a difference in people’s lives, the response was overwhelmingly affirmative. Many candidates of both parties on the campaign trail have committed themselves to pursuing such a course.

Perhaps the one remaining hope for positive change will not come from carry-over party leaders or their burned-out incumbent holdovers, but from the roughly ten dozen new members. This newly anointed frosh contingent can claim a strong mandate to work harder and better on real problems that working Americans have been clamoring for, but that the current Congress has either shunned, flubbed or punted. Keep an ear out for sounds of optimism and new directions that may emanate from the bipartisan new member orientation this week.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief-of-staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

images.caption: New members of the 120th Congress gather for the first day of new member orientation at the Capitol, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Allison Robbert)

articles.title: White House lawyer vows to fight ‘tooth and nail’ against ‘inappropriate’ investigations
articles.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf vowed Wednesday that he will fight “tooth and nail” against Democratic lawmakers pledging to open sweeping probes into the Trump administration next year, claiming their investigations are “inappropriate.” “They can’t investigate for the purpose of inflicting pain on government officials,” Scharf said on “Rob Schmitt Tonight” on Newsmax. “They can’t…
articles.body:
White House counsel Will Scharf vowed Wednesday that he will fight “tooth and nail” against Democratic lawmakers pledging to open sweeping probes into the Trump administration next year, claiming their investigations are “inappropriate.”

“They can’t investigate for the purpose of inflicting pain on government officials,” Scharf said on “Rob Schmitt Tonight” on Newsmax. “They can’t investigate things for their own self-aggrandizement. These are blatantly inappropriate uses of Congress’s power.”

“We’re going to see what happens in January, but we’re ready to fight tooth and nail here if that’s the road they want to go down,” he added.

Scharf said that since the midterm elections, there had been an “explosion” of new and incumbent Democrats “talking about subpoenas and investigations for blatantly unlawful purposes,” though Democrats vowed to conduct oversight on the Trump administration if they won either or both chambers of Congress while on the campaign trail.

The White House counsel said it was crucial that the administration “at the outset … set the tone” and accused Democrats of bringing back the “lawfare” President Trump faced before he was reelected in 2024, saying he hoped the party would have “learned a lesson from that.”

Trump was in the midst of several legal cases ahead of his 2024 victory, becoming the first former president to be found guilty on all counts of falsifying business records to conceal alleged affairs during his 2016 campaign.

“The only thing they [Democrats] achieved was putting President Donald J. Trump back in the White House where he belongs,” Scharf added.

Scharf’s comments come amid a back-and-forth with incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who warned last week after the Democrats’ midterm victories that the Trump administration should “ lawyer up ” after the start of the 120th Congress.

The White House lawyer clapped back this week, telling Garcia that the investigations and subsequent subpoenas could amount to criminal activity .

“Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end,” he wrote in a letter to Garcia.

The California Democrat even name-dropped newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Wednesday in connection with the incoming probes, saying he “ should be preserving documents .”

Garcia and other Democratic lawmakers accused the administration of hiding things and emphasized their constitutional authority to conduct checks and balances.

“So, we believe we have the right and we have been empowered expressly in the Constitution to make sure the president obeys the law,” Rep. Stephen Lynch (Mass.), an Oversight Democrat, said on CNN. “This is pretty basic, and so that’s the core function … and I speak on behalf of the chairman in this respect, I’m sure.”

When asked about Scharf’s threat to investigate Democrats in response, Lynch said, “ Come at me, bro .”

images.caption: White House staff secretary Will Scharf watches as President Trump signs executive orders in the Oval Office of the White House, Jan. 23, 2025, in Washington.

articles.title: Huang surrenders CEO spot amid affairs scandal
articles.summary: Presented by American Meat Producers Association 🏛️ Plus: Blumenthal ballroom bustle {beacon} It’s Thursday. Yes, only Thursday. What a week. In today’s issue: Jensen Huang steps down A second Starshield slowdown Warren to take on Wall Street Ballroom drama Programming note: We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker filling in for Cate today. Please send your…
articles.body:
It’s Thursday. Yes, only Thursday. What a week.

Programming note: We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday morning following the revelation of two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an executive who reported to him.

The company, a powerhouse in the AI tech industry, announced his departure, adding that Colette Kress , executive vice president and chief financial officer, will take over as CEO in the interim.

“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia wrote in a press release.

Bad for business: The AI tech giant was trading shares at $243.37 on Oct. 6. But the bombshell reports have tanked Nvidia’s stock price.

Following Huang’s resignation, individual shares fell to $148.80, a 14.4 percent drop from Wednesday.

Early Wednesday evening, they dropped below $160, which was their lowest mark since June 2025.

What happened? The CEO on Sunday admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, following an Oct. 29 report from The New York Times that alleged he had been romantically involved with Alice Huang , a suspected Chinese spy and former executive at the Singaporean-based AI chip firm Megaspeed.

President Trump threw his support behind Jensen Huang, telling reporters, “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

An open secret? As The Hill’s Laura Kelly wrote , “Trump, at the last minute, brought [Jensen] Huang on board Air Force One to travel to Beijing in May — after Secretary of State Marco Rubio informed him the U.S. had sensitive intelligence that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported.”

The revelation has led to concerns about potential threats to national security and calls from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle to investigate.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) called for Jensen Huang’s resignation Wednesday night, telling CNBC’s Megan Cassella , “I can’t believe we are even considering him not resigning. I mean, I do feel that strongly about it.”

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.), who is on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote Monday on the social platform X, “I’m pushing to investigate Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether our national security was compromised.”

Russian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday said Ukrainian military units reported significant Starshield satellite communication disruptions for several days, which have affected the front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

“This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia,” Zelensky said on X . “We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little.”

Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, also saw a slowdown in October. Ukrainian officials said the speed had been capped, cutting off drones and other equipment moving faster than about 100 mph.

It was later reported that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the slowdown .

What’s the deal?: The new disruptions come after the end of two-day peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brokered by the U.S.

A Ukrainian official said there was no mention of disruptions during the talks, and it’s not clear who made the decision, per Reuters .

Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not pass the House on Tuesday, in part due to unexpected traffic that stymied a handful of Democrats and prevented them from making it to the floor.

Beep beep: Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) on Wednesday shared a social media post apologizing for missing the vote.

“I am so sorry. There is no one who is more disappointed in myself than me that I was not here that the moment that gavel dropped, as the Republicans were trying to bury this impeachment of Pete Hegseth,” she said.

Four other Democrats — Reps. Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), Marilyn Strickland (Wash.) and Brittany Pettersen (Colo.) — pinned their absences on traffic . There were 11 total Democrats who missed the vote.

Safe, for now: Hegseth’s role is protected for now, but only until Democrats take over the House and Senate come January.

The Defense secretary also has an ally in new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Democrats are divided on how to handle Hegseth going forward. Some are pushing to bring another round of impeachment articles, while others urge for more time.

“We need to take a long, hard look at what makes sense,” Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair, said Wednesday, according to Punchbowl News . “I think Hegseth has committed impeachable offenses. I think he should be removed, [but] what’s our best approach to achieve our broader objectives?”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has signaled that Smith would be one of the leaders in charge of any Hegseth impeachment proceedings next year.

The White House called the Tuesday vote a “massive victory” and said Trump and his team would not allow Democrats to “smear and demean an American patriot” like Hegseth.

Rep. Jim Himes (Conn.), the House Intelligence Committee’s top Democrat, advised his Republican peers to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) during the lame-duck session, believing it’d be difficult to pass in its current form during a Democratic-controlled Congress.

“I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck because it’s, you know, it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year, and, you know, I think they heard the message,” Himes told The Hill.

FISA gives the government free rein to spy on what it deems foreign threats, but as The Hill’s Rebecca Beistch writes, “A growing number of Democrats, however, argue that the U.S. must rein in spy powers — citing distrust of President Trump’s use of such a powerful intelligence tool as well as Americans’ privacy rights.”

Blumenthal and the ballroom : Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) was warned on Wednesday by a top federal prosecutor to keep records related to his investigation into donors for Trump’s $400 million ballroom project .

Aaron Reitz , the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, wrote in a Wednesday letter that Blumenthal’s investigation harassed private citizens and violated the constitutional rights of those who donated.

Reitz added that there would be “significant legal consequences” should the Connecticut senator not preserve records, adding in a post on X, “I’m taking the first step to stop this abuse of power.”

Blumenthal shot back, calling the threat “baseless.”

“This investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Admin attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity,” the Democrat wrote in his own post on X .

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is expected to lead the Senate Banking Committee in the 120th Congress, a position that would allow the progressive lawmaker to take on corporate America.

“Accountability is coming. If you’re a Wall Street executive, Big Tech CEOs, giant corporations that have been cheating people, you should be worried,” Warren said this week at a conference in Washington, D.C.

A banking committee aide told The Hill the Massachusetts senator hopes to “use the power of oversight to hold Donald Trump, his administration, and his cronies accountable for making life unaffordable for working people in order to line their own pockets.”

Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine) told The Hill he has his sights on joining the committee and advised Warren to focus her efforts on affordable housing.

At least five people were shot in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington, D.C., early Thursday, with at least one fatality. Police issued a shelter-in-place order and are responding to multiple locations in the neighborhood, roughly a mile north of the White House.

The Interior Department announced its plans to sell public lands to “states, localities and Tribes” between 2026 and 2023. It added in its strategic plan that it intended to “consolidate its workforce” but did not provide further detail.

Trump on Thursday blamed Senate Republicans over midterm losses, calling their moves “devastating.” He pinned it on the SAVE America Act, which passed the House but not the Senate.

articles.title: White House counsel says Supreme Court delivered ‘generational win’ on presidential firing power

articles.body:
White House counsel Will Scharf praised the Supreme Court’s June decision strengthening presidential firing power as a “generational win,” saying Thursday it righted what he viewed as a “historic constitutional wrong.”

“A president who can’t control who’s exercising the executive power that is vested in him, that’s a cabined presidency,” Scharf said during the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Convention in Washington.

Scharf was referring to the Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in Trump v. Slaughter , which allowed President Trump to sack Federal Trade Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter — a Democratic appointee.

The ruling held the president had authority to fire the heads of most independent federal agencies at will, upending a nearly century-old precedent that had historically insulated those bodies from political interference.

Scharf said that decision, which fell along ideological lines, corrected a “very, very poor and quite ancient precedent.”

“The Supreme Court did a masterful job,” he said. “Really got it right.”

articles.body:
Longtime conservative pollster Kellyanne Conway knocked Republican ad spending in the 2026 midterms, which many Republicans lost , calling it lighting “billions of dollars on fire.”

“And you know, in this town, candidates often lose, but consultants always win. They skim 15, 20 percent off the top, quote, ‘legally.’ But you’re not reaching people where they are. We have screens, social media, streaming,” Conway said Wednesday on Fox News’s “The Ingraham Angle.”

“Nobody’s home watching these TV ads. And by the way, we lit billions of dollars on fire. And if you keep running that same ad in my living room, now I’m angry with you. You’re irritating me as if I didn’t hear you the first 50 times. So, there’s a lot to unpack there,” she added.

In last week’s elections, Republicans lost both House and Senate control for the next Congress. Democrats also won in areas where they have faced historic disadvantages, including Kansas and Texas.

The GOP also faced an uphill battle this election cycle, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down.

According to a mid-October report from The Hill’s partner network NewsNation, this election’s sum of ad spending, as well as ad reservations for later on, had climbed to more than $10 billion. The spending, per AdImpact, topped the cash put into the 2022 and 2020 elections.

Late last month , Trump announced that more than $400 million would be spent by his political operation in support of Republican midterm candidates. The Republican National Committee also said it was transferring $50 million to groups in an attempt to shore up its congressional majorities.

articles.title: Dear new member: Welcome to Congress. Now you can deliver on affordability
articles.summary: Former House leaders Cheri Bustos and Joe Crowley advise newly elected members of Congress to prioritize solving economic affordability issues, such as energy costs, housing shortages, and financial scams, over partisan ideology.
articles.body:
Congratulations! You won. Now comes the hard part.

In the next few weeks you’ll get your office lottery number, participate new member orientation, and more invitations than you can count. Everyone will have advice about which caucuses to join, which fights to pick, and which issues should define you.

We have some advice of our own: before Washington tells you what kind of member of Congress to be, remember what voters sent you here to do.

Between us, we spent 30 years in the House, both in leadership. One of us flipped a Republican seat in a district President Trump carried. The other served in a Democratic stronghold for two decades. We came from very different districts, but we both know that voters are quick to judge whether you are working on their problems or Washington’s.

Voters were not subtle this year. Ask them what they wanted Washington to talk about, and the economy won by a wide margin , with cost of living the single most common answer. Life costs too much, thanks to gas prices, tariffs and chaos in Washington. Electricity rates have risen 33 percent in five years. The country is short 5 million homes . Scammers stole a record $15.9 billion from Americans last year. Families feel those pressures every month in their utility bills, rent and mortgage payments, grocery budgets, and bank accounts.

That is your assignment: Work on those national problems first!

And, by the way, it is bigger than simply bringing a few prices down. Lasting affordability also requires an economy in which paychecks can keep up, businesses want to invest and hire here, and families have a real chance to get ahead. You should be asking a basic question of every major policy choice: Will this make it easier or harder to build, hire, invest, and afford life in America?

That question can also help you navigate one of the first temptations you’ll encounter as a new member of Congress.

Washington is full of movements, factions and interest groups eager to sign you up. They come with energy, attention, donors, and a ready-made political identity. We understand the appeal. But many of you just won highly competitive districts, including places where voters backed the other party at the top of the ticket. Those voters did not send you to Washington to adopt somebody else’s ideological checklist. They sent you to solve problems. So, start with the problems they can see and feel.

Get more energy onto the grid: Winter is here, energy costs are rising, and Americans want results. Thousands of energy projects, from transmission lines to power plants to battery storage, are stuck waiting years to connect to the grid. These delays have real consequences: projects cost more, investment and jobs go elsewhere, and consumers don’t get the relief they need. The Senate’s bipartisan permitting bill would be a boon for local economies and energy projects. If the current Congress doesn’t finish the job, the next one should.

Borrow from a bipartisan playbook: You probably spent part of your campaign promising voters that you would work with anyone who had a good idea. Now you have to prove it. The Build America Caucus released a bipartisan agenda that offers more than 60 proposals aimed at making it easier and cheaper to build housing, energy, infrastructure and childcare capacity. You will not agree with all of them. You shouldn’t have to. The point is the approach: start with the bottlenecks making everyday necessities scarce and expensive, then find people in both parties willing to remove them. Bipartisanship is not the goal. Solving the problem is. But on many of the biggest affordability challenges, you will need both parties to do it.

Turn the housing bill into actual homes: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act showed Congress can still pass big, bipartisan bills. But families cannot live in a legislative accomplishment. They need homes they can afford. Your job is to make sure the bill is funded and implemented quickly, and then to take on the barriers that make homes too slow and expensive to build. Judge success by what happens in your own backyard: Are more homes getting built? Are they being built faster? Can more families afford them?

Treat scams and fraud like the pocketbook issue they are: Scams rarely get talked about alongside housing and energy, but they should. Americans lost $15.9 billion to scammers last year, and with technology rapidly evolving we can expect that number will only grow. For a family that gets cleaned out by a scammer, that is not an abstract law-enforcement statistic. It is rent, groceries, retirement savings or a down payment that is suddenly gone. From the SCAM Act to the GUARD Act , Congress has already shown there is bipartisan appetite to strengthen fraud prevention. Build on it. Protecting people from having their money stolen is about as straightforward an affordability agenda as Congress can have.

And whatever issues you choose, start now.

Your constituents may not follow every committee markup or floor debate, but they will pay attention to your first votes, your first bills, and the issues you choose to spend talking about.

Two years from now, the important question will be whether the people who sent you to Congress feel like they can breathe a little easier. Did their electric bill stop climbing? Are there good jobs in their community? Can their kids imagine buying a home? Is starting or growing a small business a little easier?

Those are harder achievements to fit into a viral clip. They are also much closer to what voters hired you to do.

So welcome to Congress. Learn where the good coffee is. Join some caucuses, make some friends — the kind who will work across the aisle to get things done.

Cheri Bustos, a U.S. representative from Illinois from 2013-2023 and former chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, is president of Next American Era . Joe Crowley, a former U.S. representative from New York from 1999-2019 and former chair of the House Democratic Caucus, is a senior advisor to Next American Era.
